t: Guides and reference for Ara 3D Gen, the open-source generator for realistic, rigged and animated 3D human characters. Try it at ara3dgen.com. Getting started Self-hosting: install, update, build, deploy, the command line, and the tests Command line (ara3d): npx ara3d builds characters in any project, no clone needed; character files and schemas JavaScript library (ara3d): createCharacter() builds rigged, animated three.js characters in your own web app or game Embed a character: <ara-character> puts a live, animated character on any web page with one tag AI assistants (MCP): Claude, Cursor and VS Code make characters for you with npx ara3d mcp Using characters in your engine: Unity, Unreal, Godot, Blender and the web Making characters Bodies, clothing and looks: the data behind the bodies, detail levels, clothing, hair, beards, tattoos and earrings Faces, expressions and lip-sync: blend shapes, expressions, teeth, blinking, talking and lip-sync mappings Animations: every clip, motion capture, vehicles and props, weapons Rigging: skeletons, skin weights, rest poses and the weapon socket Exporting: the Export panel and the file formats Making films Ara Studio: direct films of up to five scenes, with up to five characters in 70 sets, with dialogue, sound effects, music and Assist, and export an MP4 Playing games Ara Play: missions, campaigns, arcade races and endless runs, with downloadable games Hosting your game: Publish online and its limits, and other places to host a downl

Ara 3D Gen runs entirely on your machine: in the browser, or headless from the command line. It works on Windows, macOS and Linux, and needs Node 20+ and git. The app runs in any current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.

--depth 1 downloads only the current files (about 50 MB) instead of the full history; drop it if you want every past commit, or run git fetch --unshallow later. On Windows, run the same commands in PowerShell, Command Prompt or Git Bash.

Re-run setup-assets after every update. New versions can add or change generated assets (for example new eye colours), and the app falls back to the old ones until you do. If you have local changes, commit or stash them before git pull. Each release lists what changed.

Set BASE_PATH=/sub/path/ when hosting under a sub-path, such as GitHub Pages. Site videos (media/ara-play-promo.mp4 and media/ara-studio-reel.mp4) are kept out of git, in the repository's media release, so re-rendering them never grows the repository. scripts/media.json records which version the site uses, and the build downloads any missing video into public/media/ and checks it (npm run media:fetch). Set ARA_SKIP_MEDIA=1 to build without them; the pages then show the posters. The Terms (terms/index.html) and Privacy Policy (privacy/index.html) name the operator of ara3dgen.com and its contact address. If you host your own copy, put your own details in them. The whole site is static files, and all the character work runs in each visitor's browser, so free static hosting scales with traffic. ara3dgen.com runs as a Cloudflare Worker that serves dist/ as static files, and static-file requests are free and unmetered. wrangler.site.jsonc sets it up: change its name and routes to your own Worker and domain, run npx wrangler login once, then npm run deploy:site, which builds the whole site, checks that dist/ has every part of it (pages, docs, schemas, media) and only then deploys. dist/ holds about 1,700 files, more than the dashboard's 1,000-file upload accepts, so it deploys with Wrangler. Generate characters without opening a browser, for batch jobs, CI or asset pipelines. Outside this repository, use npx ara3d, which needs no clone. Inside it: Every exported zip includes the character's params.json, so any character can be regenerated or tweaked later.

test:gltf, test:ui and test:studio need Chrome, Chromium or Edge (set CHROME=/path/to/browser if it isn't found). The scripts/blender_*.py scripts import exports into Blender and render previews; Blender is optional.

The motion-captured clips are baked into src/core/anim/clips/mocap-data.ts, which is committed, so you don't need the source recordings. To change them, edit scripts/mocap-takes.ts, run npm run setup-assets (it downloads the takes into vendor/mocap/cmu), then npm run build-mocap. See Animations.

Studio needs no server API or API key: sets, music, sound effects, recording and voice effects all run in the browser. Microphone recording and video export need HTTPS or localhost. Serving it: the build ships the compressed music in media/music/ and the sound effects in media/effects/, each with its credits. Serve .mp3 as audio/mpeg, .wasm as application/wasm and .mjs as JavaScript. Every file is under Cloudflare Pages' 25 MiB limit. The speech model: typed dialogue downloads the Supertonic 2 model (about 265 MB) from Hugging Face the first time it's used, pinned to revision 75e6727618a02f323c720cba9478152d4bc16ca4 of Supertone/supertonic-2. It isn't part of the build. To serve it yourself, copy that model directory to a CORS-enabled host (object storage or a model host), keep its licence with it, and set VITE_STUDIO_TTS_MODEL_URL before building. The directory needs: onnx/tts.json and onnx/unicode_indexer.json onnx/duration_predictor.onnx, text_encoder.onnx, vector_estimator.onnx and vocoder.onnx voice_styles/F1.json, F2.json, M1.json and M2.json The speech runtime (about 14 MiB, single-threaded, no cross-origin isolation headers needed) loads only when speech is generated. The character builder and normal Studio playback never load it. Rebuilding music and sound effects: the compressed files are committed, so a normal build doesn't need the originals or FFmpeg. To regenerate them, install FFmpeg, put the original recordings in music-for-ara/ and sound-for-ara/ at the proje

The home page plays media/ara-studio-reel.mp4 and the README shows it as a GIF. Both are cut from the films in src/studio/examples/reel.ts (the same films Studio's Assist offers as examples). To regenerate them after changing a film, install FFmpeg and a supported browser, then run: The first command renders each film with Studio's MP4 export, plus a screenshot of the editor, to out/studio-expansion/; REEL_SCENES=2,5 renders only those films. The second keeps the part of each film listed in REEL, speeds it up slightly, joins the films with short crossfades and the music, and ends by zooming out into the editor. It writes the MP4 and its poster to public/media/, and a silent GIF of it for the README to docs/media/ara-studio-reel.gif. Run npm run media:publish to upload the new video to the media release and record it in scripts/media.json, then commit that file. The Ara Play section plays media/ara-play-promo.mp4, just under a minute of Dead Drop, a demo campaign kept in scripts/promo/dead-drop.json. To regenerate it: The first command plays each shot in the real game in Chrome, with bots driving the hero, and records it at 4K to out/promo/; PROMO_SHOTS=rescue,city records only those shots. The second cuts them to the timeline in scripts/build-play-promo.ts, with captions, transitions, the game's own music and an end card, and writes a 1080p video and its poster to public/media/, plus a 1440p master for uploading to video sites at out/play/ara-play-promo-master.mp4. No Blender round trip is needed: the exports load directly. Engine Use Notes Unity FBX Imports natively; the Mixamo bone names map to the Humanoid rig. Tick Loop Time on looping clips. GLB in Unity needs the glTFast package. For lip-sync, see Faces (uLipSync, Meta's lip-sync plugin). Unreal 5 FBX The skeleton has no separate root bone above Hips (like Mixamo), so Unreal's root-motion setup may need one added. Blend shapes import as morph targets. Godot 4 GLB Loads the rigged, animated GLB directly. The Godot starter walks and runs a character with the keyboard and sets its expressions. Tick Mark looping clips in their names in the Export panel: clips are then named Walk-loop and so on, which Godot imports as looping automatically. Rhubarb Lip Sync works for dialogue. Web (three.js, Babylon.js, PlayCanvas) GLB Loads directly. npm run test:gltf proves this for three.js: it exports through the real pipeline, loads the file with the stock GLTFLoader + AnimationMixer in headless Chrome, and checks every bone of every clip against the generator. Results for all four rig variants: within 0.04°, with exact root positions, and the skinned mesh deforms. Blender GLB or FBX Both import with the rig, animations and shape keys. scripts/blender_*.py show scripted imports. Every engine: Looping: glTF has no loop flag, so set looping clips to loop. Root motion: loops play in place unless you export with Root motion. Props: parent weapons and other props to the WeaponR bone (see Rigging). Vehi

The sidebar has two modes, switched at its top. The app remembers which one you use. Quick build is the guided mode, and where new visitors start. You build a character by tapping options, and it updates as you go. Summary: a sentence at the top describes the character in plain words: "An athletic 35-year-old African man in a business suit, with cornrows and a short beard." Each highlighted word jumps to the step that changes it. Steps: Body: gender, age, build and height. Heritage: African, Asian, Caucasian or mixed. This also sets the skin, face and eye colour. Outfit: 44 styles, from everyday wear and suits to uniforms (police, security, nurse scrubs, paramedic, doctor's white coat, lab coat, airline pilot, flight attendant, hard hat and hi-vis, army medic, racing jacket and clown among them), bridal/evening wear, traditional dress, warriors and beachwear. Each has a picture. Colours: fabric and colours for whatever the outfit lets you change, plus a custom colour. Hair & face: hairstyle, hair colour, facial hair, eyes and expression. Extras: glasses, hats (a hard hat among them), jewellery, earrings, tattoos, a bag and something to hold. Vehicle: pick one of fourteen vehicles to preview its matching riding/driving action. Choose a body/coat colour, Standard/Sport style and finish; Detailed has trim/mane and seat/tack colours. On foot returns to idle without a vehicle. Vehicle selection follows the active animation, including choices made in the animation bar. Action: play

LLM Assist in the builder header creates a single character from a description. It works like Studio's Assist: Describe the character, or pick one of the Ideas. Optionally start from the current character. Write the character with your own AI key (Your own AI and voices), or Get the JSON: Copy guide (or Save as .txt) and give it to any AI assistant. Without a key, the builder sends nothing automatically. Review and build: paste the assistant's whole reply (the JSON is found inside it) or open a file. A summary card shows the name, age, outfit, hair and extras, and any problem comes with a fix request to send back. Ask Ara, in the bottom-right corner, can also make or change the character in a chat; the result is built straight away, with Undo. The guide includes the installed asset IDs, all body and face controls, clothing and fabric options, equipment, presets, rig and detail settings, a JSON schema and a valid example. Character input uses {"kind":"ara-character","version":1,"preset":"The Adventurer","params":{"name":"Desert explorer","ageYears":34,"hair":"cornrows","carry":"backpack"}}. A preset is optional; omitted parameters keep preset values or the builder defaults. Supplied arrays and maps replace their base values. Use ageYears (12–90) or normalized age, not both. Full .params.json exports can also be opened. Invalid fields, asset IDs, ranges and garment patterns are rejected before building. Build character updates the normal builder controls and mesh. Realism comes from data, not hand-built shapes. The generator uses the MakeHuman anatomy dataset, which has been CC0 (public domain) since 2020: Base mesh: an artist-made, animation-ready human (13,378 quads). Morph targets: 935 targets. Macro controls (gender, age, muscle, weight, height, proportions, ethnicity, breast) blend across a lattice of targets, exactly like MakeHuman. 219 detail sliders (head shape, nose, mouth, eyes, ears, chin, cheeks, torso, limbs…) add targets on top. Left/right pairs are merged into one symmetric slider. Proxies: eyes, eyebrows, eyelashes, teeth, tongue, 10 hairstyles, 12 outfits, 6 shoes and 2 hats. Each vertex is fitted to a triangle of body vertices (.mhclo), so clothing follows any body shape. Skin under clothing is removed to prevent poke-through. Textures: 20 photo-based skins (young / middle-aged / old × African / Asian / Caucasian × male / female), picked automatically diffuse and normal maps for clothes, and alpha textures for hair and lashes 11 eye colours: MakeHuman's 9, plus dark brown and black-brown, the most common shades There are 63 presets, including the original athletes, professionals, warriors and game characters plus a resort guest, lifeguard, paramedic, nurse, flight attendant, airline pilot, road worker, dispatch rider, street racer, police officer (USA), MMA fighter, mob boss, clown, masked robber, getaway driver, security guard, motorcycle cop, army medic, doctor, lab scientist, explorer, chef, photographer, DJ, baske

Level Body Typical triangles, dressed Low MakeHuman game proxy (~1.6k quads) ~25–50k Medium Full base mesh ~45–65k High (HD) Catmull-Clark subdivided body + clothing ~130–170k Low simplifies the body; clothing and hair keep their detail, so they make up most of a low-detail character. A full gown takes more (The Bride is about 90k at low and 110k at medium).

Choose a full MakeHuman outfit, an outfit set, or Separate pieces: Outfit sets: tee & baggy jeans (with a cap, Cuban chain and sneakers); a gold bikini (triangle top with halter and back ties, string bottom; the cups size themselves to the bust); an orange prison jumpsuit (collar and lapels, button placket, DOC prints front and back, rolled sleeves and trouser cuffs, worn and dirty) with a canvas backpack and worn sneakers; a pastel suit (single-button jacket with notch lapels and a close-fitting collar, pressed trousers with creases) over a tropical-print resort shirt (its collar laid over the jacket's), with layered gold chains, aviators and horsebit loafers; a white thobe (stand collar, buttoned placket, cuffs) with a keffiyeh and agal, a long gold chain, gold watch and signet ring, and leather slides; a tailored pantsuit over a satin silk blouse with pointed pumps and a structured handbag; a black clerical shirt with a tab collar under a long overcoat, with a silver cross, leather gloves and oxfords; an elegant suit and tie (MakeHuman's elegant suit with the suit, shirt and tie colours editable, plain or striped tie). Yoruba women's wear: ankara gown with flutter sleeves; ankara peplum top and pencil skirt; aso-ebi lace top (puff sleeves, double peplum, pearls) and maxi skirt with a gele. Each set shares one pattern and colour pair, comes with matching jewellery and high heels, and its pieces are also listed under Tops, Jackets and Bottoms. Tops: tank top, football shirt

Hairstyles: MakeHuman hair, plus generated buzz cut, punk mohawk (liberty spikes, shaved sides), cornrows and box braids. These follow every head shape and take their own Hair colour. Facial hair: stubble, mustache (alone or over stubble), goatee, short beard or full beard, with a Beard colour. Beards are hair cards (alpha-masked strips, the usual game approach) over a stubble layer. With facial bones on, they follow the jaw. Tattoos (adults 18+ only): tribal armband, full sleeve, forearm bands, chest piece, back piece, and Yoruba-style cheek marks, with an ink colour. Earrings: studs, small hoops or big hoops, in gold or silver. Tattoos, stubble and shaved scalps are painted into one RGBA "Skin details" texture in the body's UV space: Placement: the texture sits on a thin copy of the skin it covers, 0.4 mm above it. Fit: designs are defined on the unmorphed base mesh, so they keep their shape on every body. Speed: the texture is cached while you move sliders.

Topless and bottomless (no underwear) are only possible for characters aged 18+. Under-18 female characters always get a top, and every under-18 character keeps underwear. Bodies are anatomically neutral (no genital geometry).

Every character has 34 facial blend shapes (morph targets): 20 for expressions and 14 for speech. They're built from MakeHuman's CC0 expression data and blended by the character's ethnicity mix, so they fit every face. The expression shapes follow Apple's ARKit names where they match: Eyes: eyeBlinkLeft/Right, eyeWideLeft/Right, eyeSquintLeft/Right Brows: browDownLeft/Right, browInnerUp, browOuterUpLeft/Right Jaw and mouth: jawOpen, mouthSmile, mouthFrown, mouthPucker, mouthPress, mouthStretch, mouthUpperUp Nose: noseSneerLeft/Right

Nine expressions: neutral, happy, laughing, angry, sad, crying, surprised, afraid and determined. The chosen expression is the resting face in the viewer and in every exported clip: the blend shapes' default weights in GLB and FBX, baked into the mesh for OBJ.

MakeHuman's CC0 teeth (six variants, picked under Expression) and tongue. Upper teeth: fixed to the skull. Lower teeth and tongue: they rotate with the jaw whenever a shape opens it (jawOpen, the open speech shapes). They're skinned to the Jaw bone, so they also follow an animated jaw in an engine. Closed lips: faces that rest with the lips slightly apart get them closed, so a neutral face never shows the teeth.

Blinks and glances: clips blink and glance around with the eye bones. Faces that match the action: many clips also show it on the face: effort when jumping or getting up, and pain when hit a squinting aiming eye with rifles and pistols smiles when waving, cheering and laughing, and sobbing when crying half-closed eyes after a death Blinks close fully on every face: each character's blink is calibrated so the lids just meet. MakeHuman's closure would otherwise overshoot and fold the lid. Blinks in exported clips sit inside clips of 1.8 s or longer, so loops stay seamless. The live preview blinks on every clip. In an engine, short loops (walk, run) can get blinks from a separate face layer.

GLB: sparse morph targets with extras.targetNames and animated weights. FBX: a BlendShape deformer with one channel per shape and DeformPercent curves. Blender, Unity, Unreal, Godot and three.js read both. Turn off Facial blend shapes in the Export panel to leave them out; the expression is then baked into the mesh. Speech mouth shapes can be left out on their own: they add about 0.7 MB per medium-detail GLB, or 1.5 MB at high detail.

The 14 speech shapes (visemes) use the Oculus / Meta names that lip-sync tools output: Shape Sounds viseme_PP M, B, P viseme_FF F, V viseme_TH TH viseme_DD D, T viseme_kk K, G viseme_CH CH, J, SH viseme_SS S, Z viseme_nn N, L viseme_RR R viseme_aa, viseme_E, viseme_I, viseme_O, viseme_U vowels Rest (sil) is every shape at zero. The jaw, lower teeth and tongue open with the shapes. The Talk clip (Emotes) loops a stretch of babble with head nods and brow raises on stressed syllables, for background chatter and previews. To lip-sync real dialogue, drive the shapes from audio: Tools that output Oculus visemes (for example Meta's lip-sync plugin for Unity and Unreal, or Ready Player Me-style pipelines): map each viseme to the blend shape of the same name, viseme_<name>. Rhubarb Lip Sync (offline, from an audio file; works with any engine, including Godot): map its mouth cues A → viseme_PP, B → viseme_kk (or viseme_SS), C → viseme_E, D → viseme_aa, E → viseme_O, F → viseme_U, G → viseme_FF, H → viseme_nn, X → rest. Vowel-based tools (for example uLipSync in Unity, which detects A, I, U, E, O and N): map A → viseme_aa, I → viseme_I, U → viseme_U, E → viseme_E, O → viseme_O, N → viseme_nn. Blend between shapes over about 50–80 ms rather than switching, and keep each weight at 1 or below; the Talk clip does the same. The full set of 52 ARKit shapes for iPhone face capture is planned: see issue #11.

There are 248 clips. The character loads playing Idle. The animation bar at the top of the viewport has quick buttons (Bind pose, Idle, Walk, Run), previous / next, and All animations, a drawer with search and categories that keeps the character in view. These clips are recorded performances from the CMU motion capture database, retargeted onto each character: Walk, Walk backwards (the same performance reversed), Slouch walk, Run and Strafe left/right. Strafes keep their recorded feet and pelvis with a more upright upper body. Carry walk, Head-load walk and armed locomotion use these recordings with arm IK layers; Model walk uses the recorded Walk with the legs closed. All five turns use CMU 69_17's turn-in-place steps, played at twice the captured speed: 0.95 seconds for 45°/90° turns and 3.6 seconds for a full turn. Right turns mirror the performance; 45° turns adapt the quarter-turn heading. The named angles are exact and finish standing in the new direction. Jump and Low punch, including their recovery. Jump, Running jump and Low punch finish in the upright Idle pose. Cry. Sit down and Sit idle (Stand up is Sit down in reverse). The retargeting: Alignment: limbs are aligned to the recording's rest pose. Calibration for the body: arm hang, stance width, flat planted feet, and each actor's neutral head position. Loops: close seamlessly. Floor contact: the feet keep it, and the toes bend rather than dipping through the floor. The takes and cuts are listed in scripts/mocap-takes.ts. npm run build-mocap bakes them into compact data (src/core/anim/clips/mocap-data.ts), so the app, the exporters and the tests have them without the source files.

Choose a prop under Carry. Props that clips hold have their own rigid joint, export in GLB/FBX/OBJ, and animate in GLB and FBX. Set Weapon: None for two-hand holds. Pick up (ground) (3.4 s): look down, reach forward, squat with the hands clear of the knees, close both hands on a low object, then lift with the legs. Grip at about 1.5 s; the clip ends in the first pose of Carry idle. Put down / drop (ground) (3.4 s): the reverse of pickup. Lower the object to the floor around 1.6 s, release it, then return upright. Chain Carry idle/walk → Put down → Idle. Use / press (1.65 s): reach with the right hand, press with the extended index finger around 0.88 s, then retract. Open door (2.8 s): reach for a handle on the right, turn the latch around 1.0 s, pull through a 32° arc, release and return. The hinge is to the character's right. Animate your door to match the handle path. Push (2.6 s): reach with both open palms, brace in a staggered stance and drive forward, then recover. The main effort is between 1.15 and 1.65 s. Carry idle (3.6 s loop) and Carry walk: a two-hand hold of a roughly 40 cm-wide object in front of the torso, wrists 46 cm apart with palms facing inward (scaled to the character's height). Carry walk is the recorded Walk about 15% slower, with its footfalls, hips and stride distance. Box / parcel is 42 × 32 × 34 cm at reference height, with cardboard and tape colours and a shipping label. When equipped, ordinary Walk, Run, backwards/slouch/model walk, strafes, turn

Take a picture uses the camera worn on its neck strap (accessory Camera on a neck strap, as on the Photographer): both hands take it from the chest and lift it to the right eye, the left eye closes, the shutter fires twice, and the camera goes back on the chest. The camera has its own joint, so it moves with the hands, and the strap stretches with it. Without the camera the hands mime it. Talk with gestures, Phone call, Texting, Look around and Sweep are loops for background characters. In Phone call the character talks in two bursts, with the mouth moving and the free hand gesturing, and listens in between. Lean on wall folds the arms, rests one foot on the wall and expects a wall about 20 cm behind the heels. Clap, Dance (groove) (a step-touch at 120 bpm) and Dance (party bounce) (alternating raised hands) loop. Point and Thumbs up raise the hand and hold; Bow goes down and back up. Wave keeps the head and eyes facing forward. Cheer raises the fists to head height once every 0.8 seconds, with a soft bounce in the knees. Laugh loops every 4.8 seconds in two bouts that fade into a breath, with matching facial timing; Laugh hard is motion-captured, a bigger laugh that leans back and doubles over.

Handshake is played by both characters at once, standing face to face 75 cm apart, each a little to the other's right so the right hands meet; they reach in, shake three times and let go (2.6 seconds). In Studio, Stage the cast → Handshake places the two and ends both timelines with the handshake, starting together. Elsewhere, stand the second character 0.75 m in front of the first and 0.1 m to their right, turned to face them (at 1.8 m height; scale with the characters), and start both clips together. The hands meet for characters of similar height.

The water surface is the floor plane: swimmers float with the body below it and only the head and shoulders above. The builder shows see-through water while a swimming clip plays, and weapons are hidden. Tread water stays in place. Swim forward (front crawl), Swim breaststroke and Swim backstroke carry their speed in travel: 1.1, 0.75 and 0.9 m/s (backstroke travels head first). Dive into water (2 s) crouches on the bank, springs out head first, glides underwater and surfaces, about 3.5 m forward. Climb out of water (2.4 s) starts treading water facing the bank: hands on the edge, press up, knee on and stand, about 0.9 m forward onto a bank at water level. The dive and climb-out move around an even travel, so they line up with root motion and stay close to place without it.

Hands and feet are solved onto fixed holds, so nothing slides while the body moves. Each clip is built against a standard prop (metres at 1.8 m height, from the character's starting position, facing forward). The clips play the same with or without it: Props next to Root motion shows or hides it in the builder, and the export panel includes it as a separate static file (GLB, FBX or OBJ) sized to the character, with the same origin. Use it as is, or put your own ladder or wall at the same spot: Clip Prop Movement Climb ladder up / down Rungs every 30 cm (the lowest 45 cm up) in a vertical plane 36 cm ahead, 44 cm wide Up 0.5 m/s, down 0.43 m/s (loops) Vault over obstacle 90 cm high, 35 cm deep, near face 1.1 m ahead 2.8 m forward in 1.2 s Ledge hang Wall face 26 cm ahead, top edge 2.15 m up In place (loop) Climb up ledge The same wall 2.15 m up and 0.62 m forward in 2.8 s, ending standing on top On the ladder each hand moves with the opposite foot. The vault plants the left hand on top and lifts both feet over it. The hang keeps the legs straight below the hips. The climb up starts from that hang, walks the feet up the wall, presses over the edge onto straight arms, steps the right foot up and stands. A hanging body rises only as far as it needs for its hands to reach the edge, so the hang fits every arm length. Movement is carried in travel: play the clips with root motion, or move the character yourself at that speed, and the hands and feet stay on the prop. Hand-carried bag

Fighting stance is a boxing guard with the left foot forward. Punch combo (a jab, a cross driven off the back foot and a hook), Front kick, Roundhouse kick and Block start and end in it. The roundhouse pivots on the planted front foot. Sword combo (a diagonal cut, a backhand cut and an overhead chop) and Sword thrust (a lunge) start and end in Sword idle. Attacks and reactions are separate clips: time a hit or block on the other character to match. Cover clips hold a rifle and are built against a cover wall 1.1 m high, 58 cm in front of the crouched character: Take cover (1.2 s) starts from Rifle idle, takes two steps (0.46 m, carried in travel, with the feet planted) and crouches with the muzzle up. Cover idle keeps the head below the top of the wall and glances along it. Cover fire (2.4 s) rises, brings the rifle down over the wall, fires three shots and ducks back into Cover idle. The wall is a stage prop like the climbing props: Props shows or hides it, and the export includes it as a separate file placed for Cover idle (Take cover starts 0.46 m further back). Rifle hits and deaths keep the rifle at low ready through the hit. In the deaths the support hand lets go and the rifle is laid flat beside the body, clear of the floor. The body ends where Death (fall forward / backward) ends, so Get up follows. Gunshot reactions are unarmed and the bullet lands 0.05 s in: Clip Length Reaction Shot in the head 1.5 s The head snaps back and the body drops, falling backward. Shot in

The football clips kick with the right foot while the left stays planted: Clip Length Move Shoot (football) 0.95 s A long stride on to the left foot, the knee cocks back and the laces meet the ball at 0.3 s, following through high. Pass (straight) 0.7 s A short backswing and a firm swing straight through the ball, which leaves at 0.22 s. Side pass left / forward / right (inside foot) 0.75 s The thigh turns out so the toes point outward and the inside of the foot meets the ball at 0.24 s. To the left the leg swings across the body; forward it swings straight through; to the right the body opens on the planted left foot. Receive ball (inside foot) 0.7 s The thigh turns out and the inside of the foot meets a pass at 0.2 s, then gives with it to kill its pace. Chest control 0.9 s Lean back with the arms wide and clear, cushion the ball on the chest at 0.25 s and let it drop to the feet. Pick an assault rifle, pistol, sword, combat knife or grenade under Props. Weapons are held in the right hand on the WeaponR socket (see Rigging), and the viewer switches to the matching idle. Aiming: firearms are fitted to the aiming pose. The barrel lines up with the chest's forward axis, and the rifle's handguard sits under the support hand. Pistol aim (one hand) uses a lower wrist, a relaxed shoulder and a relaxed free arm. Locomotion: pistol and rifle walk, run, sprint and strafes use recorded locomotion beneath their weapon holds. Sprint retimes the recorded run, including root velocity, to keep the stride distance. Crouch walk has its own low gait. Hands stay on the weapon: two-bone arm IK places the right hand first, then the left hand onto the rifle's handguard wherever the rifle is. The left hand slides along the handguard if a pose would over-stretch the arm, so the hands stay on the weapon on every body and skeleton. Grips: fingers curl toward the palm, detected from each hand's joints, so fists and grips close correctly on A- and T-pose binds. Grenade: throw_grenade (2.2 s) releases the grenade at 0.82 seconds; it follows an arc to the ground while the thrower recovers upright. Your own props: the shooter clips work without a weapon, with your own prop parented to WeaponR.

Choose a riding or driving animation and its vehicle appears, fitted to the rider, in the builder and Studio. Show vehicle controls visibility. Choosing the sports car, SUV, pickup, tank, jet or helicopter with untouched colours applies its factory

Search Board or Alight. Every vehicle has an entry/exit pair (1.6–2.2 seconds); the convertible, sports car, SUV and pickup have separate driver and passenger pairs. Entry starts upright beside the vehicle, moves over the saddle or gunwale, through a hinged car door or the motorboat's gate, and ends in the fitted riding pose. Exit reverses it and finishes upright. Jet (2.8 s): from the pilot's right, where the canopy opens. Tank (4.2 s): up the tread steps onto the hull and down through the roof hatch, which closes over the driver. Use Board SUV → Drive SUV → Alight from SUV, for example. Give entries and exits their full clip length with movement off. Limbs keep their lengths on all three rigs and both bind poses. Human clips and matching prop animations export together; each fitted vehicle/occupant role is one prop file containing its riding and door animations.

Equip a pistol, rifle, sword or knife and choose a riding or driving action. Mounted wielding keeps the seat, legs and left control hand; car windows lower and both horse reins stay in the left hand. Canoe, kayak and rowing strokes pause while armed. Boarding and alighting hide the weapon. The tank driver, swimmers and aerial actions keep weapons hidden. Builder and game exports use the default wield pose; Studio adds per-action aim and fire (see Armed riding), and code can pass weaponPose, weaponYaw and weaponPitch to Animator.frame/bake.

Helicopter: Fly helicopter seats the pilot at the controls; the cabin has four doors for a pilot and three passengers in Studio. Jet: the jet clips carry their own motion in the builder and exports. Taxi jet on runway rolls along on its wheels; Take off jet (6 s) accelerates, rotates and climbs to a demonstration height while the gear folds; Pilot jet flies with gentle banking; Land jet (6 s) descends with the gear down, flares and rolls to a stop. In Studio the jet follows the film's route and Flight height instead. Bail-outs: Bail out of jet with parachute and Jump from helicopter with parachute (2.6 s) take the occupant out through the open right-hand side, clear of the airframe, and turn them belly-down into the pose that Skydive continues. Equip the parachute rig. In the builder the aircraft holds a safe height while the occupant leaves it. Game engines supply aircraft movement and altitude; the exports carry the pilot pose, controls, doors, rotors and gear.

The driver sits enclosed under the closed roof hatch with hands on the levers, and the tracks run. Fire tank machine gun stands the driver in the open hatch with both hands on the spade grips of a roof-mounted machine gun. Only the head and shoulders show above the gun shield; the gun traverses slowly and fires in short bursts with a muzzle flash.

Each mechanical vehicle has tumble_MODEL (3 s): a controlled 360° roll with the rider attached, returning to the upright riding pose. Keep movement off and leave extra clearance. Road vehicles (convertible, sports car, SUV, pickup, motorcycle, bicycle) have two crash escapes. In both, the driver's door opens and the empty vehicle slides on, rolls over away from the driver and comes to rest upside down; its motion is exported on the prop joints. Crash and roll out (crash_MODEL, 3.6 s): the driver dives out to the left, shoulder-rolls and stands about 3 m away, facing the original heading. Crash and fall down (crash_fall_MODEL, 3.4 s): the driver is thrown out, lands hard and tumbles onto their back, ending in the starting pose of Get up (from back).

The Aerial category has skydive, parachute_deploy, parachute_glide and parachute_land. Equip carry:parachute for the pack, a harness fitted over the clothes with straps over both shoulders, a striped canopy and suspension lines. Deployment takes 2.4 seconds; landing takes three seconds and ends in the upright idle pose. Only the canopy and line joints scale; the skeleton keeps its dimensions. Game engines supply altitude and physics; Studio supplies an editable descent.

Forward roll (roll_forward, 1.3 s) crouches, tucks and rolls over the back to standing. Side dodge left/right (dodge_left, dodge_right, 0.9 s) push off and land low on the near leg with the guard up. All three carry root motion in travel, so engines can play them in place or moving.

Keyframed clips are defined once (src/core/anim/clips/, one file per set). Each bone is posed in its own frame (X = flex forward, Y = twist, Z = side), on an "animation rest" with relaxed arms and nearly straight elbows. Hand targets are given relative to the chest (most clips) or to the floor (HandTarget.space: 'floor', for hands on something fixed, like handlebars, a broom or a ladder rung). HandTarget.tip targets the index fingertip instead of the wrist, using the rig's own finger length. Sample.feet places the ankles on floor-space holds the same way, and Sample.ikWeight eases a hand onto or off its hold. Root.yaw, pitch and roll turn the whole body (a dive rolls it on to its side). Sample.plant keeps a foot where it stood in the clip's first frame on each body, so turning hips and twisting stances (punches, kicks, sword cuts) don't slide it. One evaluator: src/core/anim/evaluate.ts drives the viewer and both exporters, so one clip works on every skeleton type and on A- or T-pose binds, and the preview matches the export exactly. GLB has one glTF animation per clip (30 fps, rotation channels plus root translation), and FBX has one AnimationStack (take) per clip. scripts/blender_anim_check.py imports the files into Blender and renders key frames of every action. To add a clip, see CONTRIBUTING.md.

Characters are rigged automatically, with no markers to place: The skeleton is built on the generated body's joints. MakeHuman's CC0 skin weights are mapped onto it. Every clothing, hair and accessory vertex then gets weights: proxies through their reference vertices, and garments through the base mesh or the nearest body vertices. Weights follow through subdivision. Option Choices Skeleton Game rig (65 bones, Mixamo names; retargets to Mixamo / Unity Humanoid / Unreal), lite (25 bones, no fingers), full MakeHuman (163 bones incl. face), none. Each also gets a WeaponR socket bone (below). Facial bones jaw + eyes (on by default; the eyes glance around in every clip) Rest pose A-pose (natural) or T-pose (re-posed with linear blend skinning) These options live in the Export panel.

Every rig has a WeaponR bone under the right hand, centred in the closed grip. Its +Y axis runs out of the top of the fist (the grip and blade axis), and +Z points toward the knuckles. Parenting a prop to it is how games usually attach weapons, so you can swap weapons in the engine without re-exporting the character.

GLB: a joint hierarchy, inverse bind matrices, and JOINTS_0 / WEIGHTS_0. FBX: LimbNodes, Skin/Cluster deformers and a bind pose. ZIP: adds <name>.rig.json, the bind pose in an engine-neutral form. scripts/blender_rig_check.py imports the exports into Blender and checks that posing deforms the mesh correctly.

An equipped grenade adds a rigid root named Grenade. It follows WeaponR until the 0.82-second release in Throw grenade, then animates independently. Attach a separate grenade prop to Grenade when using that baked motion. The parachute adds ParachuteCanopy and ParachuteLine0 through ParachuteLine13. Its pack and harness (fitted over clothing, with straps over both shoulders into the pack and a chest strap) follow the chest; only the prop joints receive deployment scale channels. Import scale animation in GLB/FBX. Do not include the prop joints in a humanoid retargeting bone map. The tiny packed rest geometry fits inside the pack, so static exports retain the packed appearance.

The export bar always shows what you're about to get, for example 📦 FBX · Rigged + 3 anims, with a Download button named after the exact file. Click the summary to open the Export panel: What to export Static model: mesh + textures. Rigged model: + skeleton and skin weights. Rigged + animations: + the clips you pick. Skeleton: game rig (65 bones, Mixamo names), lite (25) or full MakeHuman (163); an A- or T-pose bind; optional jaw and eye bones; facial blend shapes and speech mouth shapes (see Faces). Animations: tick clips by category (▶ previews each one), then choose One file, all clips inside or Zip: one file per clip. Per-clip files follow Unity's model@clip.fbx convention. They're skeleton-only unless "Include the mesh" is on. Root motion makes walk, run and strafe travel instead of playing in place. Loop names: Mark looping clips in their names names them Walk-loop and so on. Weapon (when the character holds one): In the hand: one file, with the weapon skinned to WeaponR. Separate prop file: the character without the weapon, plus <name>_<weapon>.glb/.fbx. The prop's origin is at the grip, so it attaches to WeaponR with zero offset. Stage props (when climbing or cover clips are selected, or one is previewed): props/<name>_ladder, _obstacle, _ledge or _cover as static files in the chosen format, sized to the character and sharing its origin where the clip starts (for cover, where Cover idle plays). Untick it to export only the character. Format: GLB, FBX, OBJ (static onl

Format Units Notes .glb metres glTF 2.0, PBR materials, textures embedded, alpha mask for hair and lashes .fbx centimetres Binary FBX 7.4, quad topology, textures embedded (Unity, Unreal, Blender) OBJ (_obj.zip) metres .obj + .mtl + textures/, quad topology .zip — All of the above plus params.json (to regenerate), preview.png, README and LICENSE All formats use +Y up, with the character facing +Z and the feet at y = 0. scripts/blender_check.py imports exports into Blender and renders previews. For per-engine advice, see Using characters in your engine. Grenade motion uses the independent Grenade root after release. For a separate grenade file, attach it to Grenade to preserve the baked trajectory. Parachute deployment uses scale and translation channels on its own prop joints; GLB/FBX include those channels, while static OBJ keeps the pack closed.

Studio turns Ara characters into short films with dialogue, sound and music. Open Studio in the character builder's bottom toolbar, or go to /studio/. It's an early preview: a film has up to five scenes, each up to 60 seconds long with up to five characters.

An animated Quick tour of Studio opens once the first set is ready. It highlights the real controls and demonstrates selecting, dragging, keyboard movement, turning, elevation and orbiting, then covers the timeline, cameras, sound, text, Assist and export. Use Back / Next or Left / Right to move through the guide; Skip tour or Escape closes it. The illustrations leave your film and Undo history untouched. The guide adapts to small screens and respects reduced-motion settings. Replay it from Quick tour of Studio in the left panel, or press ? with the preview focused. Dismissal is remembered in this browser. A recovered text, sound or Assist dialog stays open; the first-use tour waits until you close it.

Left: locations, the cast, their equipment and the quick tour. Centre: the film preview, the film's scenes, and the open scene's timeline. Right: the selected action, placement and camera settings. More room for the picture: Expand (or F) hides the side panels and the timeline rows. Drag the bar between the preview and the timeline to resize them; double-click it to reset. Both are remembered. Use the top-bar Undo for any edit, including moves, camera changes and the title. Space plays or pauses. To start afresh, click New in the top bar. Choose Save & start new to download the current project (including attached speech), or Start new to replace it immediately. Cancel keeps your film. A new project has one idle character, one wide camera shot and no text or sound; it saves on this device as usual. Undo brings the previous film back, including after a reload.

Search 70 sets, or filter by Studios, Workplaces, Homes, Leisure, City, Outdoors and Travel. They include executive and open-plan offices, a boardroom, a classroom, a newsroom, bedrooms, a living room, a kitchen, beaches, pools, a hotel lobby, a café, a forest trail and a harbour. There are also hospital and police rooms, a military base, a prison cell and yard, public and private bathrooms, a highway, a neon-lit street, a neon alley, a daylight alley, a football stadium, fine dining, a nightclub, an elevator and a church. Travel has four vehicle interiors: a train carriage, a city bus, a private jet and an airliner cabin. The camera looks from the front of the vehicle towards the back, so seated passengers face it, and every seat is a real seat. Each has an open area for standing scenes: the train's vestibule, the bus's standing area by the middle door, and the jet's and airliner's entry areas by the door. The views through the windows are painted, and the vehicles stand still. Each location has its own layout, with clear acting space, and its chairs, pews and benches are real seats. The highway and base have long driving routes; outdoor sets extend across a 360 m area with paths, landscaping and waterfronts, and characters can be placed up to ±200 m on X/Z. The stadium has a 68 × 105 m association-football pitch without crowd or players. Doors, toilets, taps and lift controls are scenery. Assist includes the layouts and staging notes; plan movement around obstacles yourself

Add characters: bring your exact character from the builder, or pick an Ara preset. Add character grows the cast to five. New characters start in a free spot and the others stay where they are. Select: a film opens with nobody selected. Click a character in the picture, or their name under The cast. The selected character gets a blue ring and a name tag. Click the background, press Escape or use Deselect to clear it. Equipment and placement say so if you try to use them with nobody selected. Move: Drag a character across the floor, or choose Click to place (or Shift-click the ground). Arrow keys move the selected character 0.1 m, relative to your view. With the preview focused, hold Ctrl (or Command ⌘ on Mac) with Left/Right to turn 5°, or Up/Down to raise or lower 0.05 m. Shift is also supported as an alternative. Selecting a character focuses the preview. Releasing the modifier completes the move even if the browser misses the arrow-key release. The placement fields set the exact position, facing and height. Arrange the group: Stage the cast on the right applies Side by side, Conversation, Facing each other or Handshake when there are exactly two characters; no individual selection is needed. Handshake stands the two within reach and ends both timelines with a handshake that starts at the same moment (the shorter timeline idles first). It is hidden for casts of three to five, which you place individually, and disabled until a second character is added. The dropdown shows a

A film can have up to five scenes, played in order, so a story can move from place to place: on a bus, then a street, then an office. Each scene has its own set, cast, actions, camera shots, text and sound, and its own timeline of up to 60 seconds. The title, frame shape (16:9 or 9:16) and title card belong to the whole film; the title card shows over the first scene. The Scenes row under the play controls lists them with their lengths. Click a scene to open it; everything else in Studio then edits that scene. + Scene adds a scene after the open one, in the same set, with the same cast standing where they were, each holding an idle pose, and one wide shot. Change its set and direct it from there. Duplicate copies the open scene, with all its actions, shots, text and sound. With two or more scenes, the open scene has a name, Into this scene (a Cut, or a Fade through black of 0.4 seconds each way), arrows to move it earlier or later, and Delete scene. All scenes beside the play button plays on from one scene into the next; with Repeat, the film starts again from scene 1. Without it, play and repeat stay within the open scene. A character who appears in several scenes is built once, so moving between scenes is quick. Sound, music and text belong to each scene: music set in a scene plays in that scene only. Undo covers adding, removing, moving and renaming scenes.

The timeline has a camera lane and a performance lane for each character, all on the same clock. The Select a shot or action menu reaches very short items in longer films. Actions: choose from 248 animations, searchable by name and category. Set a duration, or use the clip's own length. One-off actions hold their last pose; looping actions repeat. Move through the set: walking, running and strafing clips can travel. Check staging finds land/water and conservative static-obstacle conflicts, but playback does not stop at walls, furniture or other characters. Give them a clear path. Sitting: seated clips use the set's own furniture. Studio moves the character onto the nearest free chair, sofa, armchair, bench, stool or log, facing the way it faces, at the right height. Drag a seated character towards another seat to switch. Sets with nowhere to sit, such as studios, beaches and streets, say so. Vehicles: choosing a riding or driving action brings its vehicle. See Vehicles. Custom cast: in the builder, Save character downloads a small .ara-character.json with all editable settings; Open character reopens it. In Studio, + Custom imports that file as another cast member, preserving the existing characters and film. Custom characters count toward the five-character limit, can be edited via Character builder, survive reload, and can be removed with Undo. Camera shots: full-body, medium or close framing, on the whole cast or one character. Limits: up to 16 actions per character, 12 ca

Each camera shot can have its own angle. Select its camera block and enable Custom camera for this shot, then set Angle, Elevation, Distance and Movement. Orbiting or zooming the preview edits the active custom shot. Disable the option to inherit Film camera defaults again. Shots without overrides use the film’s camera settings. The same cuts appear in playback, PNGs and MP4 exports. Orbit: drag the background. Alt-drag or right-drag also works over a character. Zoom: scroll, or pinch on a touch screen. With the picture focused, + and − zoom and Home resets. Rotate with the keyboard: the arrow keys, when no character is selected. Camera movement: locked, slow push-in or gentle orbit, on top of your chosen angle. The angle is saved with the film, so the preview, saved frames and the exported video match. Walls cut away when you look in from outside. Choose landscape (16:9) or portrait (9:16), and edit the film's name in the top bar; Show title in the film adds it as a caption. Selection rings and name tags never appear in saved images or videos.

Choose Text & subtitles above the timeline, then add a Subtitle, Text or Bubble. Styles: subtitle plates, outlined text, speech bubbles, thought bubbles and comic bursts. Placement: Fixed in the frame, or Follow a character so the text moves with their head. Timing: set the start, duration, size and colours. Up to 64 cues can overlap. SRT: Import SRT adds timed subtitles, and Save SRT exports them. SRT keeps text and timing only; styles are saved in the project. Text is visual only: it doesn't create speech or lip-sync.

Choose Sound above the timeline. It has three tabs: Dialogue, Music and Sound effects. Voices at the top of Dialogue lists each speaker (the narrator and every character) with the voice they use for all their lines. Change a speaker's voice and their typed lines are marked to be voiced again; recordings and uploaded audio stay as they are. ▶ plays a sample of the voice. More voices connects Gemini or ElevenLabs voices with your own key (see Your own AI and voices). Script lists the lines in time order, with who speaks, what they say and whether each has a voice. Up to 24 lines can overlap. Click a line to open it: Speaker, Starts at and What they say. How it's said (Gemini and ElevenLabs voices): pick a preset such as Whispered, Excited or Out of breath, or describe it in your own words. ▶ Play line, Voice this line (or Voice again), Use a recording… to replace the audio with a file, and Delete line. Timing, effect and mix: the line's name, voice effect (Natural, Robotic, Dramatic, Radio, Telephone or Echo), length, trim start, speed, volume and pan, and Fit length to the audio. There are three ways to add a line, all starting at the playhead: + Line: type what someone says. Voice all lines at the foot of the tab voices every line that needs it, and says what that involves first. Ara's four voices are free and run on your device; the first time downloads a speech model of about 265 MB, and your dialogue isn't sent anywhere. Gemini and ElevenLabs voices use your key. Assist in the top bar turns a description into an editable film. With your own AI key connected, it writes the film in Studio (see Your own AI and voices); without one, it works with any AI assistant you like, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and Studio sends nothing on its own. Ask Ara, in the bottom-right corner, does the same in a chat and builds the result straight away, with Undo. Describe your film, or pick one of the Ideas. Tick Start from my current film to revise what you have. Write the film with your connected AI, or Get the film JSON: Copy guide (or Save as .txt) and give it to your assistant. The guide holds your description and everything the assistant needs: the locations, character controls, animations, equipment, text, speech, sound effects, music, the JSON format, an example and Studio's limits. Review and build: Paste reply, paste into the box, or Open file. You can paste the whole reply; Studio finds the JSON inside it. A summary card lists the location, cast, length, shots, actions, text, sound and music. If something's wrong, it says what and offers Copy fix request to send back. Copy guide, Save as .txt and Build film stay at the foot of the panel. Build film shows each character as it is built, then replaces the open scene (in a one-scene film, the whole film); Undo brings the old one back. To write a film of several scenes, open each scene in turn and describe it, or use the AI assistant tools, which write whole films. Voices are prepared for you: t

The assistant can design each character with the same controls as the character builder. Use params on its own, or with a preset to start from: Or embed a builder character: put a whole character-builder reply ("kind": "ara-character") or a .params.json in the actor's character field. Don't combine preset with character. What's kept: anything left out keeps the preset's value, or the default. Arrays and maps you supply replace the inherited ones. The actor's own detail, weapon and carry win over the character's. A sound effect cue goes in the film's audio object: The normal Open button accepts the same JSON. Anything invalid (unknown presets or fields, bad camera targets, out-of-range timings) is rejected before any character is built.

Choosing a riding or driving action brings its vehicle, fitted to that character. The action’s Show vehicle checkbox controls visibility, and Vehicle appearance in Equipment edits colours, finish and styling. Model swaps in another vehicle that rides the same way, such as a danfo, van or bus for the SUV, a keke, quad bike or scooter for the motorcycle, a box truck for the pickup, or a go-kart, saloon or muscle car for the sports car. Design paints race car (with Race number), police, taxi or striped versions where the model supports them. Enable Move through the set on the operator’s action and adjust Travel speed (m/s): for example motorcycle 5.4 m/s, car/SUV 4.8 m/s, motorboat 4.2 m/s, helicopter 12 m/s and jet 18 m/s. The rider and vehicle travel together and the animation keeps its timing. Shared passengers follow automatically. Vehicles don’t stop at walls, furniture or other characters, so stage a clear route.

Choose Board…, the riding/driving action, then Alight from…. All fourteen vehicles have entry/exit actions, with driver and passenger roles for the convertible, sports car, SUV and pickup. Give each entry/exit its full length (1.6–2.2 seconds; jet 2.8 s, tank 4.2 s) with Move through the set off; they contain their own footwork. Car doors, the jet canopy, the tank hatch and the motorboat’s gate open and close with the action. A vehicle waits at its first entry from the start of the film and stays parked after exit, even when its actor moves on to another vehicle. For Ride motorcycle → Alight → Run → Board motorboat → Drive boat, the boat waits at the end of the run and the motorcycle stays behind. Reusing a vehicle identity returns to that vehicle; different identities create separate vehicles of the same model.

Give the operator a matching boarding/riding/alighting sequence. Select another character’s matching vehicle action. In Vehicle, choose Share · [operator] and select a Seat. The link applies to the whole entry/ride/exit sequence. Add waiting or walking beats to time the entry. Passengers follow the vehicle’s position, heading and movement automatically. Keep the operator stationary while anyone boards or alights, and stagger use of a single entry such as the motorboat gate, motorcycle, canoe or rowing boat. Cars use separate front doors; the SUV and helicopter also have rear doors. Occupied seats and boarding a moving vehicle are rejected with an explanation. Vehicle Occupants Convertible / sports car / pickup Driver + front passenger SUV Driver + front passenger + two rear passengers Helicopter Pilot + front passenger + two rear passengers Motorboat Helm operator + two aft passengers Motorcycle / canoe / rowing boat Rider/operator + one passenger Bicycle / horse / kayak / tank / jet One rider Passengers use a seated or pillion performance fitted to their own body. Exit leaves them on the ground while the vehicle can drive off. Assist uses per-beat vehicleId and vehicleSeat.
