Keep those fields on entry and exit too. The other aft seat is passenger-right; car and he

Choose a weapon in Equipment, then a riding/driving action. In that action’s inspector, Weapon action chooses Wield, Aim / present, Fire (pistol/rifle) or Hide weapon; Match animation wields while riding and hides during boarding/alighting. Aim left / right (°) sets the heading relative to the character: 0 forward, positive left, negative right. Aim up / down (°) adds elevation, from −45° to 60°. Both are saved per action and also work on pistol/rifle performances on foot. Canoe, kayak and rowing strokes pause while armed. The same actor can board with free hands, ride armed and get off again: Fire is a recoil performance; add gunshot sound effects at the right times yourself.

Choose Board helicopter → Pilot helicopter (fly / hover) → Alight from helicopter. On the pilot action, Move through the set gives forward travel and Flight height sets 0–30 metres above the actor’s elevation. Leave it empty for 3 m while moving or 0 m while stationary; a positive height with movement off hovers. Consecutive pilot actions on the same helicopter take off once and land once, easing between heights. Land before alighting. Passengers inherit travel and altitude, so set height only on the pilot. A grounded, stationary pilot action (move:false, flightHeight:0) can wait while passengers board. The rotors stop while boarding, waiting on the ground and parked. Leave about 4 m around the cabin for the main rotor and 6 m behind it for the tail.

The pickup has a front passenger seat and an open load bed. The tank and jet carry one operator. Tank: the driver climbs onto the hull and sits enclosed under the roof hatch. Fire tank machine gun stands them in the open hatch behind the shielded roof gun, firing in bursts; the tank can keep moving. Switching between driving and the gun eases the driver up or down. Jet: boarded from the pilot’s right, where the canopy opens. For a runway flight use Board → Taxi jet on runway → Take off jet → Pilot jet → Land jet → Alight. Taxi travels at 8 m/s on the ground. Take-off and landing (6 s each) always travel forward, about 80–85 m at 18 m/s. Take-off climbs to its Flight height (default: the following flight’s height, else 8 m); landing starts from the previous flight’s height and touches down at 3.6 seconds. In the air the jet pitches with its climb, banks gently, folds its gear and shows exhaust glow. Use a long, wide, clear runway.

tumble_MODEL actions roll the vehicle and rider together through a full 360° over three seconds and return upright. Use movement off and a wide clear area. Aircraft rolls take a Flight height (default 3 m); place a roll between flights at the same height to stay airborne. Crash and roll out (each road vehicle) has the driver dive clear while the vehicle rolls over; following on-foot actions start where the driver stood up. Crash and fall down throws the driver clear onto their back; follow it with Get up (from back) or leave them lying. The wreck stays upside down where it came to rest.

h: Aerial, swimming and stunts on foot

t: Choose Parachute / skydiving rig under Carry, then use the Aerial category: Skydive — free-fall pose. Activate parachute (deploy) — the full 2.4 seconds to pull the handle, inflate the canopy and take the risers. Use parachute (glide) — repeats with the canopy open; optional forward movement is 2 m/s. Land parachute — the full three seconds for touchdown, impact and upright recovery. The inspector’s Start height is the height above the actor’s elevation. Each aerial action descends toward the next one’s start height; the defaults are 20, 12, 8 and 2 metres. Landing reaches the ground at touchdown. Keep actor elevation 0 for a ground landing. Check the landing surface and the whole canopy path. To jump from an aircraft, use Bail out of jet with parachute or Jump from helicopter with parachute (pilot or passenger) during a flight about 20–30 m up, then Skydive → Activate parachute → glide → land. Free fall starts just below the aircraft where the occupant left it, later aerial heights shrink to fit, and the empty aircraft flies on out of the shot. The jet bail-out travels with the jet. Try the parachute descent example with Assist → Open JSON.

Choose Grenade (prop) under Weapon for Throw grenade (2.2 seconds). The grenade leaves the hand at 0.82 seconds, follows an arc and stays on the ground when the actor walks away. A later throw uses a fresh grenade.

Place swimmers inside a set’s water (beach, pools, spa, lake, harbour, yacht deck, campsite); Studio water hides the body below the surface. Start Dive into water at the edge facing the water, and Climb out of water within half a metre of the bank, facing it, with movement on for both. Check staging flags strokes that leave the water.

Climbing actions bring a prop: a ladder for Climb ladder up / down, an obstacle for Vault over obstacle, and a wall with a ledge for Ledge hang and Climb up ledge. It is placed where each climb starts and stays in the set for the whole film, so later actions continue from the top of a ledge or ladder. Consecutive ladder actions share one ladder, and a hang shares its wall with the climb up. Untick Show ladder (or obstacle, or ledge wall) on a climbing action to hide the prop for that climb; the motion stays the same. Climbs always travel. Start each climb clear of the set's own walls and furniture, facing the way it should go: the vault needs about 3 m ahead. Football actions (the shot, the passes, the slide tackle, the goalkeeper catch and dives, and picking up, bouncing and throwing the ball) bring their own football. It sits at the foot, in the hands or arrives at the keeper's hands as each action starts, and flies off on the kick or throw. Untick Show football to hide it.

Fighting stance, Punch combo, Front kick, Roundhouse kick and Block chain through the stance; Sword combo and Sword thrust chain through Sword idle with a sword equipped. Strikes don't make contact on their own: time a hit reaction or a block on the other character to match, and stand them about a metre apart. With a rifle equipped, Take cover steps forward and crouches behind a 1.1 m cover wall that Studio places ahead of it and keeps in the set. Follow it with Cover idle and Cover fire, which use the same wall. Untick Show cover wall to use the set's own cover instead. Rifle hit from front / back and Rifle death (fall forward / backward) keep hold of the rifle; the deaths lay it beside the body and are followed by the matching Get up.

Shot in the head, chest, back, stomach, leg and arm are reactions to a bullet that lands 0.05 s in. Pistol fire and Rifle fire fire 0.04 s in, so start the reaction with the shot; Cover fire fires at 0.75, 1.05 and 1.35 s. Face the shooter at the victim, and shoot Shot in the back from behind. Blood sprays from the wound, lands on the floor and, after the deaths, pools under the body. It stays in the set for the rest of the film, even if the character gets up and moves on. Untick Show blood on the action to play it without blood. The deaths end where Death (fall backward / forward) end, so Get up follows. The Bullet hit and Bullet hit and fall sound effects go with them.
Forward roll and Side dodge left/right travel when movement is on.

Automatic: Studio saves on this device as you work. A reload brings back the film, the view, your selection, the playhead, open editors, Assist drafts and your Undo history. Save project: downloads an editable .ara-studio.json. Films with recorded or generated voices save as a .ara-studio.zip bundle with the audio included (up to 128 MB). Open loads either one, on any device. Save frame: the current picture as a PNG. Film links: a link can open Studio with a film loaded, as a builder share link does with a character. https://ara3dgen.com/studio/#film=… carries the film in the link, packed the way share links are; https://ara3dgen.com/studio/#src=https://…/film.json opens a film file hosted elsewhere, on a host that lets other sites read it, such as GitHub's raw files or a gist. The film after # stays in the browser, and it goes through the same checks as a file opened from disk; Undo returns to the film you had. The AI assistant tools return these links. Export film: a 30 fps MP4 at 720p or 1080p, with sound, playing every scene in order. Save soundtrack WAV exports the open scene's audio on its own. Recordings and generated voices are stored in your browser, which can clear them; save a project bundle to keep them safe. Projects point to Ara's built-in characters, sets and sounds rather than copying them, so keep the same Ara version to reopen them exactly. Video export needs HTTPS or localhost, and a browser that can encode MP4 video (current Chrome, Edge or Safari). If sou

Lip-sync for dialogue Characters touching or holding each other, or handing over props Collisions and pathfinding Importing your own models Each character's performance is directed on its own, on a shared clock.

Sets: original geometry and textures in the source code. Music and sound effects: supplied for Ara. Credits ship in media/music/CREDITS.txt and media/effects/CREDITS.txt. The recordings keep their own rights and aren't covered by the MIT code licence. Speech: the optional Supertonic 2 model and voices are OpenRAIL-M, including its use restrictions, and are downloaded only when you generate speech. ONNX Runtime Web is MIT. Notices ship in third-party/speech/ and are linked from the sound editor. Video: Mediabunny (MPL 2.0) encodes the MP4. Every build includes its licence and source in third-party/mediabunny/, linked from the export dialog. Character assets and motion capture keep their usual terms. Hosting, the speech model and the Studio tests are covered in Self-hosting.

buildHuman() (src/core/human.ts) runs in a Web Worker in the app (src/app/worker.ts), and directly in Node for the command line and tests. In the browser (the builder, Studio, Play and the ara3d library), the worker downloads only the body shapes each character uses, from assets/web/, before building it; Node reads the full targets.pack. Morph the base mesh from the parameters: macro controls plus detail sliders. Fit the proxies (eyes, brows, lashes, teeth, tongue, hair, outfits, shoes) and grow or wrap the procedural garments. Build the face's blend shapes, calibrate the blinks, and close lips that rest apart. Subdivide for high detail. Rig: place the skeleton on the body's joints, then skin every part. Assemble one multi-material mesh. The same parameters always give the same character, so params.json (and share links) regenerate it exactly.

Studio's version 2 project separates camera shots from actor performance tracks. Up to five actors are evaluated at the same explicit timestamp, while each keeps its own actions, character recipe, placement and detail. Version 1 projects migrate to the new schema on import. src/studio/catalog.ts holds searchable location metadata. sets.ts dispatches to reusable scene-family builders and the explicit recipe registry in sets/story/; sets/builder.ts shares primitive geometry and materials within a set. Only the active set is instantiated. Set changes dispose owned geometries, materials and textures. Character changes rebuild only the affected actor, and replacement models are warmed before previous resources are released. The scene renderer fits the selected camera subject (one actor or the cast), then applies saved orbit/zoom offsets and camera motion. Preview, snapshots and video use this same evaluation. The video exporter waits for every actor's textures and prevents the preview loop from drawing during encoding. To add a location, add metadata to catalog.ts and use an existing family, or register a dedicated recipe in sets/story/index.ts. The story recipes share medical, sanitary, architectural and exterior details, low-poly repeated structures, and bounded procedural textures. Add floor-plan notes to the catalogue so Assist can stage actors in the real layout. Custom exterior recipes provide their own performance bounds so the generic outdoor extension cannot overwrite roa

ara3d generates realistic, rigged and animated characters from the command line, on your own machine. It needs Node 20+ and works on Windows, macOS and Linux. You don't need to clone this repository. The first run downloads the character data (about 50 MB) and caches it, so later runs start straight away and work offline. Characters are built locally in a few seconds each.

Command What it does ara3d export [options] Builds characters and writes GLB, FBX, OBJ or ZIP files ara3d presets Lists the preset characters ara3d animations Lists the 248 animation clips by group ara3d props Lists the weapons, carried items and vehicles ara3d new <name> [--preset P] Writes a starter character file to edit ara3d schema [character|film|game] Prints a JSON schema, for editors and AI tools ara3d --help, ara3d --version Help and the installed version

Option Meaning --preset <name> A preset, such as "The Soldier"; repeat it for several --all-presets Every preset --random <seed|a-b> Random characters from a seed, or a range such as 1-200; the same seed always gives the same person --params <file> A character file; repeat it for several (see below) --formats <list> glb, fbx, obj or zip, comma-separated; the default is glb --detail <level> low, medium or high: the mesh's detail. Images are full size at every level, as in the builder's downloads (the browser library uses 1024-pixel images below high). --animations <list> Only these clips or groups, comma-separated, such as walk,run,idle or locomotion,shooter; see ara3d animations --no-animations Rigged, without the animation clips --root-motion Walks, runs and strafes move the character forward instead of playing in place --separate-clips The model plus one file per clip, in a zip; clip files hold only the skeleton and animation (Unity's model@clip convention) --weapon <id> A weapon in the hand: rifle, pistol, sword, knife or grenade --carry <id> Something to carry, such as backpack, briefcase, handbag, parcel, head_load or phone. --animations with texting or phone_call brings the phone unless you set --carry --vehicle <id> A vehicle fitted to the rider, such as motorcycle, horse, car or helicopter; auto fits whichever vehicle the chosen riding clips need --separate-props The weapon as its own file as well; vehicles are always their own file --out <dir> Output folder; the defa

In a terminal, one status line shows what's happening (downloading with speed and time left, building, writing each format), and each finished character stays on screen. Logs and CI get each step as a plain line instead. Results go to standard output and progress to standard error, so ara3d export ... > list.txt saves only the results. The run ends with a summary of files, size, time and the full output path.

Network: the first-run download retries up to four times, with growing waits, when the connection drops, stalls (no data for 30 seconds) or the server is busy. It resumes where it stopped instead of starting again. If it still fails, ara3d prints the direct link: download and unzip the file yourself, then set ARA3D_DATA to that folder. That also works behind proxies and on offline machines. Disk space: ara3d checks free space before downloading (about 85 MB) and before writing each file, and says how much is needed and how much is free. Permissions: a folder it can't write to is named, with the setting that changes it (--out, or ARA3D_CACHE for the character data). Batches: a character that fails is reported and skipped, and the rest are still made. The run ends with how many were written and which failed, and exits with an error code so scripts and CI notice. Problems that would repeat for every character, such as a full disk, stop the run straight away. Stopping: Ctrl+C stops at once. Files are written under a temporary name and renamed only when complete, so a stopped run, a crash or a full disk never leaves a broken model. Temporary files are tidied up on the next run. Details: messages are written for people. Add --debug for the technical detail behind one.

--params accepts two kinds of file: An ara-character file: a preset plus the changes you want. ara3d new hero --preset "The Soldier" writes one: Editors such as VS Code read the $schema line and offer every field, ID and range as you type. It's the same format that the builder's LLM Assist uses, so an AI assistant can write these files too. A params.json from any export: the character's complete settings, so an exported character can be rebuilt or changed later.
Keep the small character files in version control and rebuild the models when needed. A change to a character is a one-line change that's easy to review.

A build server can make the models from the character files, so the repository holds a few hundred bytes per character instead of megabytes of 3D files. .github/workflows/characters.yml is a GitHub Actions workflow to copy: it builds every file in examples/ci-characters/characters/ and attaches the models to the run as a download. The heart of it: When it runs: the workflow starts by hand from the Actions tab, with a form for formats, detail and animations. Add a push trigger with paths to build whenever a character file changes. Speed: the first run downloads the character data (about 50 MB); later runs of the same version reuse the cache, and two characters take a few seconds. Other CI services: the same npx command runs anywhere with Node 20 or newer; cache the ARA3D_CACHE folder the way the service caches other downloads.

The schemas are published at ara3dgen.com/schemas/ and generated from the same catalogues as the apps: character.v1.json: a character, as used by --params, the builder's LLM Assist and Ara Play casts studio-film.v2.json: an Ara 3D Studio film play-game.v2.json: an Ara Play game (.ara-play.json) ara3d schema character (or film, or game) prints the schema for the installed version, with no network needed after the first run. A file can name its schema in a "$schema" field, so editors check it and suggest values as you type.

Variable Meaning ARA3D_CACHE Where the character data is cached; by default the system's cache folder (~/Library/Caches/ara3d, ~/.cache/ara3d or %LOCALAPPDATA%\ara3d\cache) ARA3D_DATA Use an assets folder instead of the download, for example public/assets in a clone of this repository ARA3D_DATA_URL Download the character data from a mirror instead of GitHub, for networks that can't reach it; the download is still checked against its checksum

The tool is MIT. The characters it makes are built from CC0 MakeHuman data and the animations come from the CMU Graphics Lab Motion Capture Database, so you can use them in commercial projects. Each ZIP export includes the full licence text.

The CLI lives in packages/cli/ and shares the generator code with the website. npm run release-cli packs public/assets (without the interface thumbnails) into a zip. If the zip changed, it uploads it to the cli-data release and records it in packages/cli/src/data-version.json, which you then commit. It then builds the CLI. The zip is deterministic, so unchanged assets upload nothing. npm run release-cli -- --publish --otp <code> also publishes the package to npm: run npm login first, turn on two-factor authentication on your npm account (npm requires it to publish), and pass the current code from your authenticator app. Raise the version in packages/cli/package.json for each release.

Put a live, animated character on any web page with one script and one tag. It works in plain HTML, WordPress, Webflow, Squarespace, Notion-style site builders, and frameworks such as React, Vue and Svelte. There's nothing to install and no 3D code to write. The script includes three.js and the ara3d library (about 750 KB compressed), and the character data loads from jsDelivr. Visitors can drag to turn the character. The quickest way: design a character in the builder, choose Share, then Copy embed code, and paste it into your page.

Use one of these: Attribute Example preset preset="The Bride" One of the 50 presets. Without any of these attributes, the element shows The Soldier share share="https://ara3dgen.com/app/#c=…" A share link from the builder: the character exactly as designed random random="42" A random character; the same number always gives the same person src src="/characters/hero.json" A character file: an ara-character file (npx ara3d new hero) or a params.json from an export

Attribute Example animation animation="texting" The clip that plays (default idle), or several in a row, such as walk 3s, look_around, talk_gestures (see below). The playground lists all 248 with their IDs expression expression="laughing" neutral, happy, laughing, angry, sad, crying, surprised, afraid or determined weapon weapon="rifle" rifle, pistol, sword, knife or grenade carry carry="briefcase" Something to carry; none takes away a preset's own bag. A texting or phone_call animation brings the phone, in place of a preset's bag, unless you set carry vehicle vehicle="motorcycle" A vehicle fitted to the rider. Without an animation, it plays the riding clip colors colors="outfit: #1d2a44; carry: #8a1c1c" New colours for outfit, top, jacket, bottom, shoes, carry and vehicle (see Colours) detail detail="low" low, medium or high. Use low when a page shows many characters background background="#20283a" A background colour. Without it the element is transparent, so the page shows through look-at look-at="pointer" pointer turns the character's head towards the visitor's pointer, wherever it is on the page. camera makes it look at the viewer auto-rotate auto-rotate Turns the character slowly orbit orbit="false" Stops visitors from turning the character zoom zoom Lets visitors zoom with the mouse wheel or a pinch. It's off by default, so the page still scrolls over the character assets-url assets-url="/ara3d-assets/" Serve the character data yourself (see Hosting the data)

List clips in animation, separated by commas, and they play one after another, blending into each other, then start again: A clip that loops (walk, idle, run) plays one cycle unless you give it a length, such as walk 3s. A one-off move (vault_over, jump, punch_combo) plays once, or as many times as you ask, such as vault_over x2.

While a character loads, the element shows a wireframe figure with a soft light passing over it, and it shows again whenever the character is rebuilt. Change an attribute and the character updates. expression applies at once, and so does a new order of animations it has already loaded. A new character, props, colours or an animation it hasn't loaded rebuild it, which takes a second or two.
The element fills the width of its container, with a 3:4 (portrait) shape. Set its size with CSS like any other element:

The element fires load when its character is ready and error when something goes wrong, such as an unknown preset. The message also shows inside the element. el.character is the loaded character, with everything the library returns: faces, lip-sync, clips and the GLB file. With a bundler, import 'ara3d/embed' registers the element. TypeScript knows its type.

Versions: ara3d@0 follows the newest 0.x release, though browsers that already have the file can keep their copy for up to a week. To stay on one release, or to get a new one at once, use the full version, such as ara3d@0.9.0. Many characters: each element draws only while it's on screen, and the character data downloads once for the whole page. Browsers allow about 16 3D views per page, so for crowds use the library in a single scene. Content-Security-Policy: sites with a strict policy need to allow https://cdn.jsdelivr.net for scripts and connections, and blob: addresses for workers, images and connections. Phones: a sideways swipe turns the character and an up-or-down swipe scrolls the page. Removing an element frees its memory. Styling the loading figure: it's exposed as ::part(figure), and the error message as ::part(status), for example ara-character::part(status) { top: 12px; bottom: auto; }. Testing on your computer: open the page through a web server, such as npx serve, not by double-clicking the file. Browsers block the embed on pages opened as files, and it says so.
There are two ways to put an Ara Play game on the web: Publish online, which is quick but temporary until you claim it, and Download game ZIP, which you can host anywhere.

Game setup → Publish online puts the game on Cloudflare for free in about a minute, with no sign-up to start. Know its limits before you share the link widely: Temporary until claimed. The game is deleted after 60 minutes unless you claim it with Claim it on Cloudflare by signing in to, or creating, a free Cloudflare account. Keep the claim link private: whoever uses it owns the game. Free plan limits. A claimed game runs on Cloudflare Workers' free plan, which allows about 100,000 requests a day. Opening the game loads each of its files, usually a few dozen requests, so that's roughly a couple of thousand plays a day. Past the limit, Cloudflare refuses visits until the next day, unless you upgrade that account to Workers Paid. A new address each time. The game lives at https://<game-name>.<random>.workers.dev. Changing it means publishing again, which makes a new game at a new address, and claiming that one too. Earlier games stay in your Cloudflare account until you delete them. After claiming, you can add your own domain in the Cloudflare dashboard. Size. Up to 1,000 files and 200 MB. Films over about 4.5 MB are stored in parts that play as one file. 18+ games. Games with 18+ characters can be downloaded but not published. Visitors may see a check. Cloudflare sometimes shows a "Just a moment…" check before the game; it passes by itself in normal browsers. For a game you want to keep, update often or share widely, use a host from the next section.

h: Other ways to host your game
t: Game setup → Download game ZIP gives you the complete game: the player, characters, textures, music and films. It doesn't depend on Ara. Unzip it and upload the whole folder, keeping every file and subfolder together, to any static web host: Host Cost How Cloudflare Pages Free, unlimited visits In the Cloudflare dashboard: Workers & Pages → Create → Pages → Upload assets, then drop the unzipped folder. Files up to 25 MiB. Upload again to update the same address. Netlify Drop Free tier Drag the unzipped folder onto the page. Sign up to keep it and update it. GitHub Pages Free for public repositories Put the unzipped files in a repository and turn on Pages. Files over 100 MB need Git LFS. itch.io Free Create a project of kind HTML and upload the ZIP as it is; tick This file will be played in the browser. Your own server Varies Serve the folder over HTTPS as static files. Films seek properly when the server supports byte ranges, which common servers do. The game needs to be served over http:// or https://. Opening index.html straight from your computer won't load its files. To try it locally, run python3 -m http.server 8080 in the unzipped folder and visit http://localhost:8080.

h: Put the game on your own page
t: A hosted game can sit inside another page, such as a blog post, a portfolio or a launch page, in an <iframe>. Paste this where the game should go and change the address and name: A picture behind Play: add background-image:url(cover.jpg) to the box's style, such as a screenshot of the game. Keyboard: keys reach the game after a click inside it. A mission pauses when the game loses focus, for example when someone clicks elsewhere on the page, and Keep playing carries on. Full screen and controllers: the allow="fullscreen; gamepad; autoplay" setting lets the game's full-screen button, gamepads and music work inside the frame. Which games to embed: your own copy on your host, or a published game you've claimed. An unclaimed game is deleted after an hour, and Cloudflare's "Just a moment…" check can fail inside a frame on another site. Phones: the snippet opens the game full page on small screens, where a 3D game in a box is cramped and uses a lot of memory. Load on your server: none. The game's files come from the host it lives on.

Ara can use your own AI and voice accounts. With a key connected, Assist writes characters, films and games for you in the app, Ask Ara chats and builds from the corner of the builder, Studio and Play, and Sound gives characters natural voices. You pay the provider directly, usually a cent or two a request. Without a key, everything else in Ara works as before, and Assist still works with any AI chat by copy and paste.

Provider Used for Keys start with Free use Google Gemini Assist, Ask Ara and voices AIza… A daily allowance for keys from Google AI Studio Anthropic Claude Assist and Ask Ara sk-ant-… — OpenAI Assist and Ask Ara sk-… — OpenRouter Assist and Ask Ara (one key for many models) sk-or-… Some free models ElevenLabs Voices (including your own cloned voices), sound effects and music sk_… A monthly allowance One Gemini key covers both writing and voices.

Open Keys from Assist (Connect a key or Change), from Ask Ara (the model button at the top), or from Sound (More voices). Paste a key and press Connect. Ara recognises the provider from the key, or asks which service it is for, then checks it with a free request and shows what it found: the models it can use, or the voices and how much of the monthly allowance is left. Assist writes with: the model Assist and Ask Ara use. The first one listed for each provider is the recommended one; prices and free allowances are shown next to each. Studio lists only the models that write films well (for example Claude Opus, Sonnet and Fable, GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Carbon); if the chosen model isn't one of them, Studio uses the provider's recommended model instead, and the builder and Play keep using the chosen one. Voice new dialogue automatically: when Assist builds a film or game, its dialogue is voiced straight away with your connected voices. Remember keys on this device: on by default. Turn it off on a shared computer and keys are forgotten when the browser closes. Remove takes a key out of this browser; Remove all keys removes every one.

Your key is kept in this browser only and sent straight from the page to its provider. Ara has no server in between and never receives your key or what you write. Every Ara app on the same site shares the keys in that browser. You can set a monthly spending limit in your provider's settings for a hard cap.

Ara explains each problem in plain words, with what to do next: A wrong or revoked key, no credit, a spent allowance or a rate limit. Busy servers and rate limits are retried automatically before Ara reports them. An Anthropic organisation key that needs a workspace: paste the workspace ID (Anthropic Console › Workspaces) when asked, or create a key inside a workspace. An Anthropic organisation that doesn't allow calls from web pages (organisations with zero data retention or certain compliance settings): the key can't be used in any web app. Use a key from another organisation, or reach Claude through OpenRouter. A restricted ElevenLabs key: allow Text to Speech, Voices (read) and User (read) for it in ElevenLabs › API keys.

With a key connected, step 2 of Assist becomes Write the film (or character, or game). Press the button and Ara sends your description with the guide to your AI. While it works, a progress bar shows whether it's thinking or writing and for how long, and facts about the result appear as they arrive, such as the location and how many characters, actions and lines it has. A large film can take a few minutes: you can close Assist and keep working, and its button shows a blue dot while it writes and a green one when the result is ready to review. When the reply arrives, Ara checks it. If something is wrong, Ara sends the problem back to the AI to fix, up to twice, before showing you the result. The review card then works as usual: check it, then Build. Stop cancels at any time. The cost of each request is shown when it finishes. Or use any AI chat instead keeps the copy-and-paste route.

Ask Ara, in the bottom-right corner of the builder, Studio and Play, is a chat with your AI. It knows which app you are in and what is open: the character, the film or the game. Ask it how to do something, or describe what you want. In Studio, Ara has the full map of the location that's open. When a message names other locations ("a rooftop chase"), their maps go with it, and the AI can ask Ara for any other location's map itself; the reply notes which maps it looked at. When Ara writes a character, film or game, it is checked and built straight away, and its card offers Undo to put back what you had. If it can't be built, the card says why and offers Ask Ara to fix it. Voices, sounds and music are extras: if one can't be made (an allowance runs out, say), the rest is built anyway and the card says what's missing, with fixes that don't call the AI again. In Studio these are Try again, Use Ara’s voices (switches the unvoiced lines to Ara's free voices and voices them in Sound) and Use library audio instead (drops the sounds that weren't made and picks the closest library music). In Play, a game built from Ask Ara loads straight away. Dialogue in Ara's own voices isn't voiced automatically from the chat, because it needs the first-time voice download. Use Voice all lines in Sound (or Generate all speech in Play) for those lines. Conversations last until the browser closes; ＋ starts a new one. In Play, Ask Ara stays out of the way while a game is being played and in full screen.

Sound's voice menus list Ara's four free voices, Gemini's 30 voices and the voices in your ElevenLabs account, your own voices first. ▶ plays a sample: ElevenLabs' own preview, or a short sentence in the voice. How it's said directs Gemini and ElevenLabs voices. Pick a preset (Whispered, Shouting, Excited, Nervous, Sad, Angry, Laughing, Sarcastic, Calm, Out of breath) or describe it in your own words. ElevenLabs works best with a word or two, such as whispers or excited; Gemini understands phrases such as warm and slow. Ara's own voices don't take direction. Sound effects and music: with ElevenLabs, Studio's Make a sound and Compose music make them from a description (see Studio). Voiced lines are saved as audio in this browser and included in exports, so a film plays the same everywhere. A film that uses a provider's voices can be opened without that key; only voicing new or changed lines needs it.

The ara3d package generates realistic, rigged and animated characters inside your own web app or game, as three.js objects. Characters are built on the visitor's device, in a background worker, so the page keeps running. The character data loads from a free CDN. Try it first in the playground: pick a character, props and an expression, and copy the code it writes. Or start from a template that runs in your browser on StackBlitz, with nothing to install: three.js game starter: a character you steer with the keyboard or by clicking the ground, walking, running and looking at you when it stops. React Three Fiber: a reusable <Character> component; click the ground to walk there. Plain HTML: characters on a page with the <ara-character> tag. Their code is in the examples folder on GitHub. It's written in TypeScript and ships its types, so editors autocomplete every option. It needs three.js 0.160 or newer, a modern browser, and a bundler (Vite, webpack, Next.js and so on) or an import map. No extra bundler setup is needed: the worker is built in.

createCharacter(input, options) takes: A preset name: 'The Soldier'. PRESET_NAMES lists all 45. A share link from the builder: design a character visually at ara3dgen.com/app, choose Share, copy the link and pass it in: A random character: { random: 42 }. The same seed always gives the same person, so a crowd of { random: 1 } to { random: 50 } looks the same on every visit. An ara-character object: a preset plus changes, the same format as the CLI's character files and the builder's LLM Assist: Character settings: the params.json from any export, or your own values. See the character schema for every field and what it means. Unknown fields and out-of-range values are rejected with a message that says what's wrong.

Option Meaning animations Clip IDs or categories, such as ['walk', 'run'] or ['locomotion', 'shooter']; 'all' (the default, 248 clips) or 'none'. ANIMATIONS lists them detail 'low' (about 25–50k triangles dressed), 'medium' (about 45–65k) or 'high' (about 130–170k); see Detail levels. Low and medium use textures up to 1024 pixels across, which look the same at web sizes and download faster; high uses the full 2048-pixel textures rootMotion Walks, runs and strafes move the character forward instead of playing in place weapon 'rifle', 'pistol', 'sword', 'knife' or 'grenade', held in the hand carry Something to carry, such as 'backpack', 'briefcase' or 'phone'. With the texting or phone_call clip in animations, the character carries the phone unless you choose something else vehicle A vehicle fitted to the rider, such as 'motorcycle' or 'horse'; it comes back in props colors New colours for parts of the character, such as { outfit: '#1d2a44', carry: '#8a1c1c' }; see Colours onProgress (label, fraction) => {}, for a loading bar assetsUrl Where the character data is served from; see Hosting the data Presets come with their own props: The Female Executive carries a handbag and The Professional Hitman a pistol. Pass 'none' to take one away, such as carry: 'none'. Choose only the clips you need. A character with every clip is about 28 MB and takes several seconds to build; with three clips it's about 7 MB and takes 1–3 seconds.

Property Meaning scene The character: a three.js Group to add to your scene animations The clips, for THREE.AnimationMixer clip(id) The clip for an ID, such as hero.clip('walk') props Props exported beside the character, such as a vehicle: { name, scene, animations }. They share the character's origin, so add them at the same position and play the matching clip on both params The character's full settings. Save them to rebuild the same character later colors The current colour of each part you can recolour, such as { top: '#5b6b3a', bottom: '#5b6b3a' } height Standing height in metres glb The character as a GLB file, for downloading or uploading dispose() Frees the GPU memory when you remove the character createCharacterGLB(input, options) returns only the GLB bytes and doesn't need three.js. Use it to save characters, send them to a server, or load them in another engine.

The colors option recolours fabric and props: Part What it colours outfit A suit, gown or other outfit made of one fabric. On a few older whole-body outfits it's multiplied over the fabric, so it can darken them but not lighten them top, jacket, bottom Separate pieces, such as a shirt worn under a suit, or a T-shirt and jeans shoes Heels, sneakers, oxfords, loafers and slides carry The bag or other carried item vehicle The vehicle's paint (or a horse's coat) Which parts a character has depends on what it wears: hero.colors lists them with their current colours, which makes it easy to build colour pickers. Parts the character doesn't have are skipped, so the same colors work across a crowd. On patterned fabric, such as camouflage, the colour replaces the pattern's main colour. For a second colour or a different pattern, set garmentStyles in the character's settings (see the character schema). Weapons keep their own colours.

playSequence() plays clips one after another, blending each into the next, and starts again after the last: A clip that loops (walk, idle, run) plays one cycle unless you give it a length, such as walk 3s. A one-off move (vault_over, jump, punch_combo) plays once, or as many times as you ask, such as vault_over x2. Steps can also be an array: ['run', { clip: 'vault_over', times: 2 }, { clip: 'idle', seconds: 4 }]. Options: { fade: 0.5 } sets the blend in seconds (default 0.35), and { repeat: false } stops on the last clip. Every clip in the sequence must be in the animations you built the character with. sequence.stop() ends the sequence and hands the mixer back to you.

locomotion() blends idle, walk and run by speed. Your code moves the character; set speed from that movement every frame, and the steps keep pace with the ground: At 0 the character stands in the idle. Up to legs.walkSpeed (about 1.5 m/s for a 1.78 m character) it eases into the walk, and between that and legs.runSpeed (about 3.7 m/s) it blends into the run. Faster than that, the run plays faster. The natural speeds scale with the character's height, so a tall character takes longer strides. Changes of speed ease in over a quarter of a second. Set { smoothing: 0.1 } for a snappier change. Use other clips with { idle: 'rifle_idle', walk: 'rifle_walk', run: 'rifle_run' }, after loading them in animations. legs.stop() hands the mixer back to you, for a jump or another one-off move. Call hero.locomotion(mixer) again to carry on.

lookAt() turns the head and neck towards a point or an object: The neck takes some of the turn and the head the rest, up to 75° to the side and 35° up or down. A target behind the character eases the head back to the front. { amount: 0.5 } turns halfway, and { smoothing: 0.4 } turns more slowly (the default is 0.2 seconds). The turn is added on top of the animation, so it works while the character walks or talks. It runs in hero.update(delta), which must come after mixer.update(delta).

Every character carries face shapes, so it can change expression, blink and talk. Expressions: EXPRESSIONS lists them: neutral, happy, laughing, angry, sad, crying, surprised, afraid and determined. A character starts with the expression in its settings. Lip-sync from audio: hero.lipSync(audio) moves the mouth with whatever plays through an <audio> or <video> element, a MediaStream (such as a microphone) or a Web Audio node. It reads loudness and the shape of the sound, so it suits voice-overs and live talking without any extra tools. It runs in hero.update(delta), and .stop() closes the mouth. Browsers start audio only after a click or a key press, so start playback from one. Lip-sync from a tool: MOUTH_SHAPES are the 14 Oculus viseme names (viseme_aa, viseme_PP and so on) that lip-sync tools output. Feed each viseme your tool reports to setMouth(). While a mouth shape shows, it moves the jaw and the expression's smile or frown eases off, so talking and expressions combine without over-stretching the mouth. Face shapes: FACE_SHAPES lists every shape, with ARKit-style names (eyeBlinkLeft, jawOpen, mouthSmile and so on), so face-capture data can drive them directly. A few clips move the face themselves, such as talk, laugh and the hit reactions. hero.update(delta) adds their movements to the expression, so an expression you set stays while they play, and blinking runs on top.

PRESET_NAMES, ANIMATIONS (each clip's id, name, group, category and whether it loops) and PROPS (weapons, carried, vehicles) are available straight away, without loading any data. Use them to build pickers.

By default the character data comes from jsDelivr, a free public CDN, through the ara3d-data npm package. DEFAULT_ASSETS_URL shows the exact address, which is pinned to the data version this release expects. A page downloads only what its characters use: the body shapes for that body, and the clothes, hair and textures they wear. The first character usually takes 2–4 MB, each different character after it adds well under 1 MB, and the browser keeps everything for later visits. To serve it yourself, for example for an offline app or a strict network:

Crowds: build a few characters, then clone them instead of rebuilding. Clones share the geometry and textures, so they cost little memory: Mix in random characters ({ random: n }) for variety, and use detail: 'low' with only the clips the crowd needs. T-pose: characters are rigged in a natural A-pose. Pass { preset: 'The Soldier', params: { restPose: 'T' } } for a T-pose, which Unity Humanoid and many retargeting tools expect. Smaller rigs: params: { rig: 'game_lite' } gives a 25-bone skeleton without fingers, for distant characters. See Rigging for every option. Mixamo and other animations: the default game rig uses Mixamo's bone names (Hips, Spine, LeftArm and so on). Mixamo files prefix their bones with mixamorig:, so rename their tracks to match, for example track.name = track.name.replace('mixamorig:', ''). Clips made for a T-pose skeleton work best on a character built with restPose: 'T'. If limbs still twist, the skeletons' bone orientations differ; retarget with a tool such as three's SkeletonUtils.retargetClip.

Responsiveness: building runs in a worker, but loading the finished model into three.js happens on the page and takes a moment for large characters. Build during a loading screen, or keep animations small. Pages opened as files: browsers block the worker on a page opened straight from disk (file://), so serve it, even locally (npx serve). Content-Security-Policy: the worker runs from a blob: address. Sites with a strict policy need worker-src blob:. Several characters: the data loads once and is shared, so later characters build faster. Versions: the changelog lists what each release of ara3d and ara3d-data contains. Licence: the library is MIT. Characters are built from CC0 MakeHuman data, with animations from the CMU Graphics Lab Motion Capture Database, so you can use them in commercial projects.

The library lives beside the CLI in packages/cli/ (src/index.ts, with the worker in src/library/) and shares the generator code with the website. npx vite build --config packages/cli/vite.lib.config.ts builds dist/index.js, and npm run test:library checks it in headless Chrome, with photos in out/library/. The developers page (developers/index.html, src/developers/) runs the library from source for its playground; after npm run build, npm run test:developers checks it on desktop and phone, with photos in out/developers/. npm run release-cli builds both packages; add each release to packages/cli/CHANGELOG.md. The library loads the ara3d-data version in packages/cli/src/data-pin.json. When public/assets changes, raise the version in packages/data/package.json, publish the data on its own with --publish --data-only, and release ara3d with --publish once npm has approved it (this can take days); ara3d then loads the new data. Until jsDelivr serves the data, --publish refuses to release ara3d; --publish --keep-data releases it anyway, still loading the data it loads now.

ara3d mcp lets AI assistants make Ara characters, Studio films and Play games for you: Claude, Cursor, VS Code's Copilot and any other app that supports the Model Context Protocol. Ask in plain words, and the assistant designs the character, builds it on your machine and writes the 3D files. Make a cyberpunk hacker with a rifle, walking and running, as a GLB for my Godot game. Give me five random townsfolk at low detail with just idle and walk. Make The Female Executive in a navy suit without her bag, as FBX for Unity. Write a 20-second film of two agents arguing in the warehouse, with a slow push-in. Make a three-scene film: she rides the bus, takes the train, then flies home. Make a rescue mission at the military base with three guards and a pickup getaway. Everything runs on your computer. The first character downloads the character data (about 50 MB, once), and the files land in ara3d-characters in your home folder unless you ask for another place. Each answer includes a link that opens the character in the Ara builder, so you can see it and keep editing. It needs Node.js 20 or newer.

Claude Code: Claude Desktop: open Settings → Developer → Edit Config and add to claude_desktop_config.json, then restart Claude: Cursor: add the same mcpServers entry to ~/.cursor/mcp.json (or .cursor/mcp.json in a project). VS Code: add to .vscode/mcp.json in your project: Other apps take the same command: npx -y ara3d mcp.

Tool create_character Builds a character and writes GLB, FBX, OBJ or ZIP files. Starts from a preset, a random seed, a builder share link, or a character the assistant designs. Takes animations, detail, root motion, a weapon, something to carry, a vehicle and colours list_presets The 63 preset characters list_animations The 248 animation clips, searchable, such as "dance" or "rifle" list_props Weapons, carried items, vehicles and expressions character_schema Every field of a character, so the assistant can design one: body, face, hair, clothes, colours and rig. It comes in parts create_film Checks an Ara Studio film of one scene, or up to five scenes in different sets, as Studio does, saves it as .ara-studio.json and returns a link that opens it in Studio, to watch, edit and record as a video. It also runs Studio's staging check on every scene and lists any place a character or vehicle walks or drives through something, so the assistant can fix the route film_guide How to write a film: the core rules (including films of several scenes), then topics on request (sets, animations, sounds, the full format), and the staging map of any set (location-map with a set's ID) create_game Checks an Ara Play game as Play does, including where everything goes on the map, saves it as .ara-play.json and returns a link that opens it in Play, to play, edit, download or publish game_guide How to write a game: the core rules, then topics on request (game modes, the map library, appearance rules)

Where files go: set ARA3D_OUT to change the default folder, for example "env": { "ARA3D_OUT": "/Users/me/game/characters" } beside args in the config. The assistant can also name a folder for each character. Offline or a fixed copy of the data: the same ARA3D_DATA, ARA3D_DATA_URL and ARA3D_CACHE settings as the command line. Updates: npx -y ara3d mcp runs the newest published ara3d whenever the assistant starts it (npm may reuse a copy it fetched a short while before). Assistants read the list of tools when they start the server, so restart the assistant app to pick up new tools; in Claude Code, /mcp can reconnect it. A fixed version: npx -y ara3d@0.9.0 mcp instead of ara3d.

Smaller, faster files: ask for only the animations you need. Every clip makes the file bigger and the build slower; a character with all 248 is about 28 MB. Licence: characters are built from CC0 MakeHuman data, with animations from the CMU Graphics Lab Motion Capture Database, so you can use them in commercial projects.

Ara Play turns character recipes and a few mission choices into a playable game. Open /play/ with npm run dev, or serve the production build. Game setup organizes creation into Mission, Cast, Challenge and Atmosphere. The mission sequence and Add mission action stay visible above every section; a persistent label names the mission and section being edited. Hero and life-budget controls are explicitly shared across the game. LLM Assist produces a complete capability guide for an external assistant and accepts its JSON for validation and preview. Five measured locations, objective chains, enemy roles, ground and helicopter extraction, combat, story cues and independent game ZIPs use the same simulation in preview and export. The creator chooses the story beats; Ara stages characters, routes, terminals, supplies and vehicles automatically.

Game setup → Mission → What kind of game? chooses the rules: Mission (the staged maps described below), Arcade race or Endless runner. Race and runner games keep the same four sections: Mission picks the circuit or course and the format (laps, or the runner's goal); Cast picks your car and the field of rivals, or the chaser, beside the usual character tabs; Challenge sets handling, boosts and pickups, or pace, obstacles and power-ups; Atmosphere keeps the music. Mission-only controls are set aside while an arcade mode is chosen. Every mode uses the same hero, cast, music, chapters, saved setups and independent game ZIP. Enemy characters drive the rival cars or play the runner's chaser. In JSON, "mode": "race" or "mode": "runner" sits at the top level with a matching race or runner object. Each chapter plays its own mode, chosen under What kind of game? while that chapter is selected, so one campaign can run a mission, then a street race, then a rooftop escape. A chapter without a mode plays the first chapter's mode and, within that mode, inherits its race or runner settings unless it sets its own. In race and runner games the sequence above the sections lists cup races or run stages, or campaign chapters when modes are mixed, and Make it yours sets the title and briefing. Each race or stage opens on a briefing card with its briefing, if one is set, and the cup or stage list with finished chapters ticked; Next race or Next stage opens that briefing. Until the creator names it,

Choose one of eleven circuits, or supply a custom circuit as 6–64 [x, z] control points in metres with a width of 10–24 m and any circuit theme. Custom loops are 400–6000 m long, cannot cross or touch themselves, and need corners no tighter than the road allows. Built-in circuits add ramps, and City Loop and Neon District have shortcuts. The course is generated from straights, corners and T-junctions in the chosen theme and gets harder with distance: shorter straights, tighter spacing and more combined obstacles. Every obstacle leaves a way through. Obstacle Way through Low barrier Jump Overhead bar Slide Gap Jump Lane blocker Change lane Moving cart Change lane Armed enemy Shoot it down your lane (F, Enter or the Shoot button), or change lane Armed enemies rise into view about 32 m ahead in one lane and walk slowly toward the runner, gun at the ready, raising it within 18 m. Cast → Armed enemies chooses which enemy appears (runner.gunman; automatic picks an armed enemy other than the chaser, and an unarmed one is given a pistol) and the runner's gun (runner.weapon; automatic uses the chapter's loadout gun, else a pistol). The runner carries that gun throughout the run and raises it to aim down the lane with each shot, legs still running. A shot travels down the runner's own lane and drops the nearest enemy within 38 m for 150 points and two coins. An enemy still standing in the runner's lane at 14 m fires once: a shield, hoverboard or boost takes the hit, otherwise the runner stumbles. Running into one ends the run. Clipping a low barrier or a bar is a stumble: the runner slows and the chaser closes in, and a second stumble soon after is caught. Hitting a blocker or cart, falling into a gap, or missing a corner ends the run unless a shield or boost is active. Revive continues the run for coins, doubling the

Cast → Player → Character moments applies to every chapter and is stored as the top-level poses ({"lookAround": true, "dance": true}, both on by default). With Look around before the start, the hero plays the look-around animation while a mission or runner briefing is open. With Dance on a win, the hero dances (the groove dance) on a completed mission, and a reached runner goal ends the run: the runner stops, the camera swings round to face them while they dance, and the results follow. Without the dance, missions end with a cheer, and a single runner stage carries on past its goal for a high score while a stage in a series ends there. Race drivers stay in their cars.

Atmosphere → Light, weather & sound sets the time of day and weather for races and runs, stored as mission.environment.time and weather; each chapter can choose its own. Dawn and dusk tint the sky and lower the sun. Dusk and night switch on every car's headlamps with light pools on the road ahead, lamp posts with pools along the circuit, and lamps and a lantern pool around the runner. Night runs keep a bright moonlit fill, a longer view and faintly lit obstacles so the course stays readable. Rain darkens and wets the road so it reflects, with falling streaks and the Heavy rain recording; fog closes in the view; a sandstorm adds an orange haze, blowing dust and the Sandstorm recording. Both recordings loop with a crossfaded seam, and filtered noise stands in until they load. Weather sound falls silent while the game is paused or the page is in the background. Thicker fog also shortens the draw distance. The lamps and pools are batched additive decals rather than real lights, so night and weather add a handful of draw calls and no extra lighting cost. Race and runner games have no companion; companion settings stay in the JSON but are unused.

Tilt steering can be switched on from the pause card on phones. The lens widens with speed, impacts shake the camera, speed lines and a soft edge blur grow with pace, boosts flash the screen and near misses briefly slow time; reduced-motion settings soften these effects. Engine pitch follows the car's speed, other sound effects are synthesised in the browser, and the music gains tempo and volume as a race goes on or a run speeds up. Both modes run fixed-step rules, draw repeated objects in batches and reuse course pieces, coins and obstacles instead of creating new ones. Choose Freight depot, Military base, Desert compound, Market street or Urban block. Each has its own solid geometry, measured starts, patrol lanes, roof positions and extraction anchors. Walls and props block movement, sight, bullets and grenade blasts. Twelve arrangements combine three staging patterns with four cover packs. Open, Balanced and Cover-rich layouts remain available. Three ready-made goals remain available: Escape: collect the key and unlock the gate, or collect vehicle keys and drive out. Rescue: free the companion and reach extraction together. With pickup extraction, the rescue unlocks the truck; there is no additional key hunt. Clear: defeat every enemy, then extract. Use starting or findable firearms. An optional briefcase or package is a required additional objective. It waits near the gate, a little further in at night, clear of the floodlight posts. Interact from any reachable side; Ara faces the item and cancels blocked approaches instead of trapping the character. Secured cargo becomes mission inventory. Choose On foot, Pickup or Helicopter extraction. Pickup challenges provide Easy (inside the compound), Standard (approximately 150 m) or Hard (approximately 300 m) routes. Longer routes include physical roadblocks, cones and ordered checkpoints; route difficulty is independent from vehicle pace. Build an objective chain replaces the fixed goal with one to eight ordered steps: Step Player action Configuration Reach Enter a marked area Optional objective

The hero, each of one to five enemies, and the companion can use presets, imported character settings or complete custom character recipes. Customize the squad together or edit individuals. Body settings, clothing and props come from the character builder; gameplay weapons come from equipment and enemy response. Optional weapon pickups and objective unlocks start the hero unarmed. Chapter completion can unlock a pistol or rifle; the strongest unlocked firearm carries to later chapters. Combat steps require a starting or findable firearm, avoiding circular objective unlocks. Shots use height-aware cover tests and stop at the first living actor. Allies block shots without friendly bullet damage. Grenades use swept flight, visible arcs, bounces and a 2.6-second fuse. Blast exposure checks solid cover; the hero and companion can be hurt by explosions. Defeated actors and their equipped guns remain

A pickup waits from the first frame and stays where it is parked; Drivable vehicle swaps it for a sports car, SUV, motorcycle, saloon, muscle car, danfo minibus, van, box truck, keke tricycle, scooter, quad bike or go-kart, each with its own top speed. Cars, vans and trucks are boarded through the driver’s door; the keke, scooter and quad are mounted like the motorcycle. A rescued companion rides in the pickup. The city district’s parked fleet mixes all of these with a city bus. Moving traffic (Off, Light or Normal) sends cars, danfos, vans, trucks and yellow taxis around the side streets in the right-hand lane: they slow for corners, queue, stop for people and the player, sound the horn when kept waiting and pull out around stopped vehicles. Moving cars block the player’s car, walkers and gunfire. Local districts have no side streets, so they have no moving traffic. With police on, the patrol chases in a marked police saloon with flashing lights. Approach the driver’s door to board. Actual body size determines cabin clearance and entry anchors. Steering keeps full lock for manoeuvring; at speed the wheel turns in more gently and the lock eases off, so fast driving carves steady arcs. Atmosphere provides Dawn, Day, Dusk and Night, plus Clear, Rain, Fog and Sandstorm. Night and adverse weather reduce guard visibility. Floodlights have measured solid posts; their lighting reach is shared with perception. A player flashlight reveals nearby terrain and makes the player easier to spot. Close contact and sound still matter at night. Choose quiet ambience, automatic ambience, wind, forest/birds, ocean, heavy rain or sandstorm from Studio’s compressed recordings. Automatic ambience uses heavy rain in rain, the sandstorm recording in a sandstorm, wind in fog or the desert, birds at a daytime market, and quiet elsewhere. Combat/movement effects include gunshots, impacts, punches, footsteps and body falls. Pickup engines use the recorded engine loop. Playback is bounded, lazy, pause-aware and respects master mute. Audio failures do not stop gameplay. Choose allowed camera views and the starting view. Players switch among permitted views with V, the camera button or the pause menu. Third person and Close follow start directly behind the character near eye height, with a slight 3° downward tilt. Players can lower the tilt to a fully level view. Orbit and Close follow support horizontal rotation and vertical tilt; fixed Overhead/Isometric views retain their intended elevation. Creators can disable rotation or zoom. Background music comes from the same compressed music library as Studio and loops during active play.

Atmosphere → Story & dialogue accepts a Studio JSON or project ZIP and renders it locally into a portable film, or accepts an MP4/WebM. Films are limited to 60 seconds and 24 MiB after rendering. Films play before/after that chapter in every mode and are skippable. The opening film plays when a mission, race or run first starts; the ending film plays when a mission is won, a race is finished or a run goal is reached. Retries and daily challenges skip the films. A missing or unsupported clip cannot permanently block the game. Add up to 24 cues triggered by mission start, a time, an objective number, detection, overwatch, reinforcement arrival, objective completion or extraction. Cues support subtitles, captions and comic speech/thought bubbles following the selected character. Text timers pause with the game. Each cue plays once per run; checkpoint retries can replay later cues. Cues can also use any recorded Studio sound effect. Enable Voice this line or Read opening briefing aloud for native device speech. Device voices vary. Generate all speech prepares selected lines with Studio’s on-device speech engine, record speech directly in Play, or attach an audio recording. Choose a voice for each line: two female and two male Ara voices, or Gemini and ElevenLabs voices with your own key (Your own AI and voices). More voices… in the voice menu connects one. Prepared speech is stored locally and exported as audio; players do not download speech models. Native speech remains a fallb

Automatic checkpoints save completed goals, defeated targets, collected supplies, ammunition, grenades, cargo and rewards together. Chain checkpoints retain completed steps. Pickup road checkpoints restore safe parked positions and ordered route progress. Retries consume a life, preserve the run’s accumulated time, and provide three seconds of protection. Active ordnance and partial actions are cleared. Checkpoints Off restarts the mission’s objectives. Campaigns contain the first chapter plus up to nine more, and each chapter can be a mission, a race or a run. When a chapter finishes, Next opens the free-roam city district before the following chapter whenever the campaign has a mission in it, whatever the modes on either side; driving to the city's marker opens that chapter in its own mode. Cups and run stages with no missions go straight from one chapter to the next. The hero, remaining life budget and strongest unlocked firearm carry forward between missions; chapters can independently choose locations, objectives, casts, atmosphere, music and story. Modes come in any order. A chapter starts from the first chapter's settings: race and runner settings stay with their own mode, and a mission chapter with a different story leaves the first chapter's objective steps behind unless it lists its own. Beginning a chapter restores its configured health/ammunition. Reloading resumes the latest unlocked chapter, with prior chapter scores and weapon unlocks. Restart campaign clears c

Ara Play's Publish online button needs a small publishing service in two parts, both on free plans: a Cloudflare Worker that does almost all the work, and one account step as a Vercel function. Cloudflare refuses to create temporary accounts for requests coming from any Worker (worker_subrequest_blocked), and its API doesn't accept requests from web pages, so that single request runs on a server outside Cloudflare. Players' games don't go into your account. Each one goes into a temporary Cloudflare account created for that player, which they can claim within 60 minutes. Cloudflare deletes unclaimed accounts. See Cloudflare's claim deployments for the platform side.

Cloudflare's provisioning and upload API can't be called from a web page, and each temporary account's API token must not reach the browser. The service relays each step and keeps that token encrypted inside an opaque session that the browser carries between requests. It stores nothing. Both parts run the same code (src/publish-service/) and share SESSION_SECRET, so a session sealed by the account step opens on the Worker. Step What the service does POST /v1/challenge Fetches Cloudflare's proof-of-work challenge. The player's browser solves it in a background thread: about 16 million SHA-256 hashes, a few seconds. POST /v1/account Runs on Vercel. Checks the game's project.json, then creates the temporary account and returns the sealed session and the claim link. POST /v1/manifest Checks the file list and opens Cloudflare's asset upload session. POST /v1/upload Streams one batch of files to Cloudflare. POST /v1/finish Uploads the fixed game server script, attaches the files and turns on the game's workers.dev address.

Allowed pages only. Requests must come from an origin in ALLOWED_ORIGINS. Rate limit. Each visitor can start up to three games a minute: through the PUBLISH_LIMIT binding on the Worker, and an in-memory count on the account step. No 18+ games. The service parses project.json and refuses any game where a character in any chapter has underwear off, nothing on the bottom half, or is a woman with nothing on top. Ara Play makes the same check before it uploads anything, so players see the reason straight away. The checked game is the published game. The manifest's project.json must have the same content hash as the copy that was checked. Game files only. Paths must be plain game files (HTML, JavaScript, CSS, JSON, text, character packs, images, audio, video and their numbered parts). Nothing may start with _ or . except /_parts.json. Each file is at most 5 MiB; a game is at most 1,000 files and 200 MB. No custom server code. Every game runs the same fixed script (src/publish-service/game-server.ts). It serves the files, joins split films with byte-range support, and adds a small Report this game link to the page.

Deploy the Worker with your Cloudflare account: Wrangler prints its address, for example https://ara-publish.<your-subdomain>.workers.dev. Create the shared settings in publish/vercel/.env.deploy (kept out of git): a SESSION_SECRET of 32 or more random characters, and ALLOWED_ORIGINS listing the pages that host Ara Play, comma-separated. Give the Worker the same secret: Build the account step and deploy it to Vercel. The first deploy signs you in and creates the project (accept the folder as it is); then add both settings for Production, using the values from .env.deploy, and deploy again so they take effect: It runs as an ordinary Node function, not on Vercel's edge network. Put both addresses in .env at the repository root, which every build reads: Without VITE_PUBLISH_URL, the button explains that publishing isn't set up and points players to Download game ZIP. Local development can publish too: http://localhost:* in ALLOWED_ORIGINS allows any localhost port. Changing SESSION_SECRET means setting it on both hosts; publishes already in progress then fail and the player starts again.

Studio's maps come from the geometry recipes that render all 70 sets. In Assist, choose Location for this film, then copy the guide or save the map as JSON. The guide contains an index of every set and the selected set’s full contract. All location maps downloads the collection. These are reference documents; do not add their fields to a film project.

Coordinates are world metres. Rectangles use [minX,minZ,maxX,maxZ]. Yaw is in degrees: 0 faces +Z, 90 faces +X, 180 faces −Z, −90 faces −X. bounds: the mapped performance area; generally ±180 m outdoors, actual rooms or conservative stage bounds indoors. land: those bounds excluding water. A floor mesh under a water surface is not navigable land. water: exact rendered surface rectangles, including shoreline and far/side extents. Remain inside the mapped performance area too. regions: rendered walkway, road, court, stage and dock footprints. A dock restores walkable land over water. Clearance does not imply a traffic rule or permission to drive through a venue. obstacles: conservative geometry envelopes with bottom and top heights, including walls, furniture, vegetation and barriers. Overpasses retain their clearance. Cutaway walls still count as barriers. seats: actual registered seating positions and facing; Y is the seat-top height. Studio retains nearest-free-seat fitting. routes: checked reference start/end poses, travel mode and clearance. Stop at the endpoint; an extension is unverified. starts: separated, checked reference world starting options for pedestrians and supported vehicles. boarding: verified reference dock approaches, standing gates, waiting vessel origins and departure endpoints. An empty array means no boarding anchor was verified. Lanes and anchors assume rig scale and anatomical boarding scale of 1. These scales can differ on real characters. Vehicle en

h: Travel is centred over the whole track
t: Actor X/Z is the centre of its complete enabled travel, not its start. Let D be the sum of each enabled local travel vector multiplied by its beat duration. Nominal displacement at time t is cumulativeTravel(t) − D/2. Multiply by rig scale, rotate by authored yaw, then add actor X/Z. To start at world S, solve actorXZ = S + rotate(scale × D/2). For local (x,z) and yaw a, rotation gives (x cos(a) + z sin(a), −x sin(a) + z cos(a)). Speed overrides affect vehicle travel, not animation cadence. Rowing travels local −Z. Adding later travel can shift earlier positions. Turn clips animate the skeleton but do not change the track's travel axes. JSON has no waypoints or per-action heading/position fields. Vehicle doorways and shared occupants modify the nominal path. An exit carries its standing offset into the next ground span. A new vehicle waits at the end of that span minus its boarding offset, from frame zero. Reusing a vehicle identity returns to its parked position; Studio adjusts the connecting span to meet the real doorways. Passengers inherit the operator’s transform. Recalculate the whole track after edits.

The shoreline runs east–west at z = −7.5, with land toward +Z and water toward −Z. Water spans x = −300..300, z = −327.5..−7.5; mapped travel stays within ±180. The walkable pier spans x = −1.2..1.2, z = −14..−4, through an opening in the rail. Decorative moored hulls sit near x = ±9, z = −11. The reference motorboat anchor uses yaw 180 throughout: Pose X Y Z Land approach 0.85 0 −3 Standing boarding gate on pier 0.85 0 −11.5 Waiting motorboat origin 2.47 0 −11.92 Water departure endpoint 2.47 0 −45 The local motorboat standing offset is (1.62, −0.42) multiplied by anatomical boarding scale. These are world coordinates, distinct from centred actor placement. Solve the whole track, including the preceding motorcycle exit and run. Native locomotion has a small lateral component; do not assume it follows a perfectly straight local-Z line. Keep the motorcycle on land, the approach on the pier, and the future boat fully in water at frame zero. Stop the operator throughout every boarding interval. Shared passengers use one vehicle identity and stagger use of its single gate. The reference anchor does not certify every custom character’s approach or stepping contact.

Check staging & location map uses the loaded characters’ scales, fitted props and boarding root footwork. It reports both sides of every action transition. Travel uses swept footprints, detecting thin barriers or water between safe endpoints. Boarding footwork and helicopter altitude are sampled at 30 fps. Parked and future vehicles are checked from frame zero. Raising an ordinary actor’s Y does not turn water into ground. The reply preview in Assist performs a provisional reference-body check. After building, run the fitted check and save its report for your assistant to correct. Each finding identifies an entity, time range and reason; selecting it seeks to that time. The report also exports each actor’s rig scale, anatomical boarding scale, height and operator-owned vehicle envelopes. With Start from my current film enabled, the guide includes these fitted measurements and positions for the unchanged cast; new or redesigned characters require a fresh fitted check. Checks are advisory against static scenery and conservative body/prop envelopes. They do not stop playback, solve routes, move the cast, simulate hand/foot collisions or check person-to-person and prop-to-prop avoidance. Furniture overlap during seated clips is intentional. Review tight contacts, boarding gaps and moving cast visually before export.
